#56361. Industry News: Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Good Deer Hunting in Bad Weather

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2664 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Good Deer Hunting in Bad Weather

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2664 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A buck is not the only creature in the woods who gets into a “rut” during hunting season.
  • In a recent development, the point is, if you wish to improve your hunting success, you must be adaptable and let prevailing conditions, rather than past practices, determine your hunting methods.
  • Before devising hunting strategies based upon the weather, it will prove helpful to examine the effects of weather on deer behavior.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A buck is not the only creature in the woods who gets into a “rut” during hunting season. Many hunters adopt a particular method of hunting and never consider changing it, even though the weather and, therefore, the hunting conditions change. For instance, many hunters automatically take to their tree stand and wait. To them, there is simply no other way to hunt. However, on very windy, cold days preceding and during the passage of a cold front, you can sit in a tree stand until you wear the brads off your britches and never see a deer. On the other hand, there are also hunters who would never climb a tree and who insist on still hunting. But on those days when the woods are extremely dry, you can walk to the next county without spotting anything.

In a recent development, the point is, if you wish to improve your hunting success, you must be adaptable and let prevailing conditions, rather than past practices, determine your hunting methods. While there is much to be stated for hunting hard and putting in a good effort, flexibility, rather than fortitude, is the key to good hunting on bad days.

Before devising hunting strategies based upon the weather, it will prove helpful to examine the effects of weather on deer behavior.

Recent findings suggest that as a rule, deer follow their normal routine of bedding, feeding, and moving throughout a wide range of climatic conditions. It is not unusual to see them feeding normally during rain or moving on breezy days. In general, scientists and observers agree about how deer act in relation to weather.

According to Al Berner, a biologist with the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources, “Under typical rainy conditions, there is minimal effect on deer — they will continue to move about normally — but during a freezing rain, they will seek shelter.”.

He also reported that deer continue their normal movements during windy days, but are careful to move into the wind in order to more easily detect danger.

According to recent reports, dean Murphy, chief of the wildlife division of the Missouri Department of Conservation, stated deer increase their activity somewhat during normal rainy days. This is largely because light is reduced to a level nearer the diurnal range. The amount of daylight on overcast days closely resembles light in the early morning or late afternoon, which is when deer normally move.

According to recent reports, A study recently completed by Scott Hygnstrom, a graduate student at the University of Wisconsin at Stevens Point, revealed some interesting data on buck movements in relation to the wind. The study was conducted with the assistance of members of the Stump Sitters, an organization that studies deer behavior. The results of the study demonstrated that, under perfectly calm wind conditions, there were fewer sightings of bucks than expected. However, under light wind conditions, there were more buck sightings than expected. As wind increased in velocity, buck sightings decreased proportionately.

Upon reflection, it seems reasonable that bucks would be more active in a light wind. The wind would make it possible for them to detect danger more easily by catching the scent. At the same time, their ability to hear would not be as diminished as it would be in a strong wind.

In a recent development, francis X. Leuth, formerly a biologist with the Alabama Department of Conservation and Natural Resources, discovered that the same holds true for whitetails in the Southern United States. Deer continue normal movements in rain and wind unless it becomes very strong or very cold. During such times, deer will hold in cover — sometimes for as long as several days.

It has been revealed that all researchers agreed that deer tend to hold up during very heavy weather, whether it be cold rain, wind, sleet, or snow. Most of them also reported increased movement 12 to 36 hours before an advancing front and immediately after its passage.

These authorities also agreed on another point: If hunters continued to hunt during bad weather instead of looking for a warm dry place to wait it out, they would be much more successful.

Before examining various weather conditions and the hunting methods best suited to coping with them, it is important to define the three types of hunting that will be recommended.

The first of these, stand hunting, involves taking a position — either up in a tree or in ground cover — and watching one area for the duration of the hunt. While stand hunting has many advantages, its primary disadvantage is that you are limited in the territory that you can cover. If deer are not moving in the area that you are watching, the hunt is over!

Walk-and-stand hunting means finding concealment on the ground and watching an area for a period of time, then moving on to a new area. The idea is to watch different kinds of areas to determine where the deer are located. It is somewhat like a bass fisherman trying to establish a pattern by fishing in different kinds of structure, depths, and locations.

Stillhunting involves intermittently moving and stopping in a slow, deliberate pattern as you move through the woods. It offers you the opportunity to cover more territory, but it also provides deer with an opportunity to spot you.

Recent findings suggest that some of the conditions that indicate a need to change hunting routines are sudden changes in the weather, days of heavy rain, windy days, and extremely dry conditions. Let’s look at them in detail and see which hunting method best fits each one.

Sources indicate that A sudden change in the weather is usually associated with an approaching low-pressure system. For some reason that is not fully understood, all wildlife seem to be more active under these conditions. It is not known for certain whether they know that bad weather is coming and are moving to areas that offer better protection, or if they are eating an extra portion to hold them over for a while. For these reasons, or for some other unexplained reason, their movements increase during these few short hours.

Sources indicate that regardless of the reasons, this type of behavior carries certain implications for hunting techniques. During an approaching front, the walk-and-stand hunter may have a slight advantage. The stand hunter usually places his stand along known trails leading to and from feeding and bedding areas. He also tends to hunt in the morning and the afternoon in order to take advantage of the early/late movement pattern. Because of frequent variations in their movement patterns during an approaching front, deer may not follow their established routines, thus lessening the chance that one will pass by when the stand hunter expects.

Sources indicate that the stillhunter is also at a disadvantage because, although the deer are more active, they are also more alert. Because they are more exposed to danger, they exercise greater caution.

Industry observers note that walk-and-stand hunting offers the best combination of stand and stalk hunting, especially if you stay in the woods all day. The best pattern is to pick a location that offers an open area — not necessarily an open field — and to watch for movement near the edges of cover. For instance, if you can find an open hardwood hollow bordered by pine thickets or honeysuckle, you may find some crossing action or movement along the borders of the thick cover.

After watching an area for an hour or so, move to another location and repeat the pattern. This allows you to cover a lot of territory during a day, and you are likely to find an area in which the deer are moving.

In a recent development, the most uncomfortable condition to hunt under is rain. If you are going to hunt in the rain, stillhunting offers some advantages. First, you can move very quietly when the ground is wet. Secondly, you can cover more territory. This is often required during rain because you have to go to the deer if they are not moving.

During periods of light rain, the deer’s behavior is hardly affected at all and there would be little need to change a preferred method of hunting under these conditions. However, if you are not skilled at still hunting and wish to learn more about it, this would be an ideal time to give it a try.

Industry observers note that if you are not an experienced stillhunter, it is a very awkward and difficult method to develop confidence in. You feel exposed and think that everything in the woods is hiding and watching you. In turn, the temptation is to try to hide behind trees, rocks, and bushes. The problem is that you always see a better place in front of you and you keep moving from one hiding place to another. Soon, you have gone through the area that you were supposed to be hunting and have come out convinced either that nothing was there or that stillhunting is a waste of time. The problem is, you were concentrating on hiding instead of on hunting.

Related: Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Deer Hunting When the Weather Finally Turns Cold.

A few points may prove helpful in learning this highly productive method of hunting. First, move as slowly as possible. Deer see movement more easily than they recognize objects. Second, when you stop, kneel down to blend into the ground cover or lean against a tree so that you are not silhouetted. And third, move less and look more. Study every area of cover and use binoculars! Look for parts of a deer such as an ear, a leg, and especially for the horizontal lines of a back or a belly among the vertical lines of trees or bushes. Many hunters think that binoculars are used primarily to see great distances, but their best use is to find small pieces of a deer in thick cover.

Probably the only thing worse than hunting in the rain is hunting when the woods are bone dry. It is more comfortable to the hunter, but it means more difficult hunting. Every movement and crunch of leaves is a signal to the deer to clear out.

Stillhunting and walk-and-stand hunting are difficult, if not impossible, during dry weather, leaving stand hunting as the most logical choice. You may want to choose a ground blind for convenience’s sake but, where it is legal, hunting from a stand in a tree enlarges the area that you can hunt effectively.

It has been revealed that even with the advantage of being able to see better from a tree stand, remember that you cannot see everything at all times. You can only see about one-third of the area at any time and many opportunities for a shot can be missed if you are not alert.

Sources indicate that if you want to prove this to yourself, think about how many times you have suddenly noticed a deer standing in the open, 15 or 20 yards from the nearest cover. It did not simply appear on that spot. The deer walked there while you were looking somewhere else. It hurts to think how many go by unnoticed.

Sources indicate that the principal way in which dry weather helps the stand hunter is that it cuts down on the area that you have to watch. You patrol the area with both your eyes and your ears. A deer can move more quietly than you can but, when it is dry, even deer will give away their position. On windy days or when the woods are wet, however, deer can slip by without a sound.

One effective technique is to locate your stand on the edge of a field or an open woodland area. You can then hunt the open area with your eyes and the thick woods with your ears, thus covering your hunting area more thoroughly.

Sources indicate that if it is not too wet or too dry, it can always be too windy. Wind has probably saved hunters more ammunition than any other weather condition. I’m not referring to those days when there is a steady breeze blowing — this can be beneficial to the hunter — but rather to those days when it is bitter cold and the wind seems to come from all directions at the same time. On these days, deer will either hold in thick cover and not expose themselves or they will pick up your scent and slip away without your ever knowing that they were there.

Using a buddy system to move deer into the open offers an opportunity to get a shot at a good buck on such days, but the plan must be carefully thought out in advance. Pre-planning not only places hunters in the most opportune positions to get the best shot, but also provides a safety measure in that they know where not to shoot.

Sources indicate that for the purpose of illustration, consider a hunting situation in an agricultural area with woods dispersed between fields. The driver should start on the downwind side of the thickest cover in the hope of moving the deer down the hollow into more open areas or across the field into the adjoining woods. If there are fingers of the land protruding out into the fields, they provide natural escape routes. Bucks in particular will cross an open area at its narrowest point.

Hunters should position themselves to cover these routes, but it is better if they take a stand across the field in the adjacent woods, rather than in the same area of woods.

Contrary to appearances, deer do not leave the state when disturbed. They leave the area of disturbance quickly, but soon resume their normal activity at a much slower pace.

It has been revealed that when a deer is jumped and makes its escape across an open area, it will likely slow down once it is out of the immediate area of danger. Often, if you take a stand along an escape route away from the jump area, this will mean a standing or walking shot rather than a quick glimpse of a white flag. Contrary to appearances, deer do not leave the state when disturbed. They leave the area of disturbance quickly, but soon resume their normal activity at a much slower pace. Hunters should be stationed at other escape points and farther down the hollow in case a jumped deer chooses to move on down the wood line rather than cross the open field.

When attempting to move deer out of cover, it is better to stop occasionally than to walk continuously. Often, a deer will watch from cover and let a hunter walk on by. If you have ever observed deer while driving, you may have seen a similar reaction. If you keep moving, they stand and watch but, if you stop, they move out. The same thing is often true of a continuously moving versus a moving-and-stopping technique of hunting.

According to recent reports, A buddy system of moving deer can be devised for any type of terrain you hunt. The vital points to remember are to use the system in an area that everyone is familiar with, to identify the stand placements carefully and, for safety’s sake, to coordinate the time and the direction of movements of each person.

Recent findings suggest that occasionally, even for those of us who are willing to modify our hunting techniques and to learn upcoming ways to hunt on bad days, there are those times when it is neither too wet, too dry, nor too windy. And on those days, even if you don’t see a deer, you can always think, “What a great day to be hunting!”.

This story, “Good Deer Hunting On Bad Days,” appeared in the April 1985 issue of Outdoor Life.

#56359. Why You Should Never Underestimate Mule Deer

Why You Should Never Underestimate Mule Deer

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3208 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

In a recent development, if you head north and east out of Salt Lake City toward the Wyoming state line you end up in some of the most stunning country in the United States. At first glance, it looks like a semi-arid range of mountains with the exposed shelves of red rock, patches of sage, and grassy benches typical of the Intermountain West at this latitude.

But once you get past the view from the winding highways that snake through this land and gain some elevation on the dirt roads that take you back to more remote areas, you’ll notice something else. These mountains give birth to a surprising number of springs, providing water that ends up supporting a vast amount of life.

The wet country reveals itself in the stands of aspen that grow thick in places you wouldn’t expect, with waist-high grass that contrasts with the blanket of drought-resistant scrub oak that covers much of the terrain.

This almost contradictory mix of moisture, cover, food, and remoteness provides a recipe for great elk and mule deer, and is the reason I’ll return to this country whenever I can, as happened a few weeks ago this fall. I was there on an invitation from Winchester Ammunition to try its newest offering, Supreme Long Range, on my favorite North American game.

It has been revealed that there are many reasons mule deer have such a strong claim on my psyche. I love the wild places they call home. The hours spent glassing them is about the most rewarding way to pass time. And I find it infinitely fascinating to watch and study their behavior.

Recent findings suggest that you see, mule deer are a study in contradiction, too. Are their numbers in decline? In many places, without a doubt. They’ve certainly struggled to maintain their hold in much of their traditional range. Housing and energy development disrupt their winter grounds and migration routes. Diseases like CWD have taken their toll, especially with older bucks. We know that blossoming herds of elk and whitetails can outcompete mulies for food and water, putting more pressure on their numbers.

But they are also resilient and, in some areas, thrive. Good numbers of mule deer live in suburban areas throughout the mountain west. And you can find them in some of the most inhospitable desert regions of North America, and tucked away in other unlikely places.

Though they can seem more docile than their high-strung white-tailed cousins, I have witnessed mule deer put on incredible displays of strength, aggression, and John-Wick-caliber willpower — another contradiction.

It has been revealed that years ago in Colorado, I watched a hunter fail to follow up his shot on a mule deer. The high-shoulder shot dropped the buck where it stood, knocking it senseless. The hunter started celebrating, thinking he had killed it, and when the deer regained its feet the hunter wasn’t ready — and the buck disappeared into the alders. I helped track the deer for several hours through the snow, following a substantial blood trail. We kept going as long as we could after dark but eventually had to call it quits.

The hunter left for the airport and I kept looking for the deer with my good friend Cody while trying to fill my own tag. Two days later, Cody and I spotted the buck tending his does, despite the grievous wound in his upper chest and one ruined leg. He was 500 yards away, skylined on the ridge, and I couldn’t get a shot off before he fled over the mountain.

According to recent reports, there was no doubt in my mind the buck was going to die from that injury, but procreation was his sole preoccupation. Despite the obvious pain, and the imminent certainty of death, he would not be deterred.

That buck spurned death, but I’ve also seen mule deer inflict it. I was hunting in southeast Montana a few years back in mid-November when the rut was in full swing. Bucks were bird-dogging does, scent-checking the ladies, cruising in search of mates, and squaring up against potential rivals.

It has been revealed that usually when two bucks face off they will posture a bit and, after sizing each other up, one will back off before things get too heated. Sometimes they will fight — those antlers aren’t just for decoration — and the vanquished male will make his excuses to be elsewhere.

In this case, the smaller of the deer lost his footing during the scuffle and fell back, rolling on his side. The larger buck lowered his head and drove his antlers into the other’s exposed belly.

The deer on his side flailed his legs in a desperate attempt to get up and escape, but through my binocular I could see the spreading circle of red in the snow as the dominant buck continued the savage attack, never letting up.

After several minutes — it felt like an eternity from my vantage — the buck’s fury was spent and he lifted his head and walked off as the other deer lay still, surrounded by his own gore.

I relate this because it is one thing to enjoy hunting, which I do, but it is another to, on occasion, experience the wild at its most raw and profound.

So, when I got this latest opportunity to test my legs and lungs in the high-country in Utah, I had hopes of encountering a mature buck, and perhaps more.

I was joined on the trip by Kyle Masinelli, the vice president of manufacturing operations at Winchester Ammunition, and a friend and work colleague of mine, Ed Friedman, the editor-in-chief of American Rifleman. Kyle was one of the architects of Winchester Supreme Long Range and a great source of information about it.

As the name implies, Supreme Long Range (SLR for short) is geared toward major-game hunting where longer shots might be in the offing, which is often the case when mule deer hunting. This new ammo uses what Winchester calls their “BC Max” bullet, which is a heavy-for-caliber cup-and-core design with an oversized polymer tip to initiate rapid expansion.

Over the summer, I shot several boxes of this fresh ammunition, chambered in 6.5 Creedmoor, with excellent results in terms of its precision and consistency.

Sources indicate that I gathered 20 shots of data with three different rifles, shooting four 5-shot groups with each. Those twelve 5-shot groups ranged in size from .53 inches to 1.10 inches. The overall average group size was .818 inches.

In a curious coincidence, the mean radius value for each of the three rifles was .32 inches, which is very good for hunting ammunition.

The three rifles I used to gather the data were Proof’s MTR Elevation FDX, which won an Editor’s Choice for best hunting rifle of the year; Seekins Precision’s latest PH3 NRL Hunter, which won an Editor’s Choice for best crossover rifle; and a Seekins Precision SIC Short Action, which won’t be officially rolled out until early 2027.

It has been revealed that for the hunt itself, I went a different route, taking a Winchester XPR chambered in 6.8 Western. The XPR has been a perennial choice of ours for an entry-level hunting rifle. It is a no-frills bolt-action that delivers good performance. In its most basic black synthetic stock trim it can be had for less than $600 new.

It has been revealed that while I’ve shot plenty of XPRs over the years, I hadn’t had as much time with the 6.8 Western. I shot this souped-up .270 Winchester a bit when it was first rolled out in 2021, but had never done a deep dive on the cartridge or taken it hunting.

I didn’t have as much trigger time with the XPR and the ammunition as I would have liked before rolling into camp, but I did establish a solid zero prior to making the drive from Montana to Utah and knew that the 175-grain 6.8mm SLR bullets were exiting my 22-inch barrel right at 2,700 fps.

Sources indicate that we were hunting with the R&K Hunting Company, which has a base camp in Coalville, Utah, and I confirmed my dope on targets they had there. With three shots, I checked my point of impact at 200, 500, and 700 yards, the bullets ringing the center of the steel each time.

Our hunting camp was another hour’s drive into the mountains, most of it off-road, and much of it pitted with craters like small bomb impacts.

But the camp itself was an alpine Shangri-La. The main lodge was a cozy wood structure where the hunters stayed, with a series of small cabins for the guides, and other out buildings, all overlooking a post-card scene of a small lake surrounded by golden-leafed quakies and distant mountains.

Those mountains were where we hunted.

In a recent development, kyle and I spent the first day with our guides, two young brothers named Keston and Kandon Mosher, glassing the heights. In the afternoon, we spotted two excellent bucks engaged in pre-rut posturing.

Sources indicate that from nearly a mile away we watched the bucks through our optics. One of the bucks appeared to have a larger, darker body and a heavier rack. The other buck was mature as well, seemingly younger, but with larger antlers. Both were stunning.

We watched them circle each other a bit in a small clearing between stands of alders. We needed to move promptly, because the cover around them was thick, it was getting late, and we were losing light.

We grabbed our packs and guns and hoofed up the mountain as fast as we could. It took about half an hour of hard climbing to get to the knob we wanted to set up on. That put us within 800 yards of where we’d last seen the deer.

Industry observers note that assuming we spotted them again, we’d make a final proposal. But that didn’t happen. We glassed the ridge until dark. We could see many of the other deer we’d been watching, but the bucks had vanished. As has happened to me so many times while going after big mule deer, they’d given us the slip.

Sources indicate that we returned to the base of that mountain ahead of sunrise, peering into the cover as the light came up. With each passing minute, we took in more ground.

According to recent reports, the mountain was actually a long, fairly flat ridge running north to south that topped out at 9,200 feet, and encompassed five separate large drainages. From end-to-end it spanned over three miles. The middle section seemed to hold the most animals, but we frequently spotted elk and deer at the northern and southern edges too.

Early on, Keston caught a flash of antler in an alder thicket not far from the top of the ridge. We all trained our optics on the spot and after a bit the lighter-colored buck stepped into the open. We easily identified him based on his coloration and the picture-perfect four-point frame he carried above his head.

According to recent reports, he was feeding on his own about 350 yards from where we’d seen him the previous afternoon. About 30 yards below him was a doe and two fawns, also munching on grass. The other massive buck was nowhere to be seen.

According to recent reports, there was no way to get to him from below. Even if we could approach from that direction without busting him he’d be out of sight until we stepped into the same clearing. That clearly wouldn’t work. Plus it would take well over an hour and a half to hike up there at which point he’d certainly be gone even if we were as stealthy as ninjas.

Instead, we hiked back down to our side-by-side and took a long looping route to the top of the ridge. From this latest vantage, the terrain presented more of a challenge than I would have guessed. Looking down, I could see benches and pockets of cover that were invisible from lower down. This included small natural ponds and abundant feed. An animal could move through that all day and never reveal itself to a hunter glassing from below.

It has been revealed that we parked well away from where we saw the buck last and snuck along the spine until we were above his feeding spot. We crept toward the edge and peered down the slope.

In a recent development, at this point the wind shifted so it was coming from directly behind us. We saw the doe and her fawns scoot out of the pocket, having clearly caught our scent.

It has been revealed that but the buck should have been between us and them, and if he followed a similar escape route, I would get a shot. We held tight for a quarter hour but saw no sign of him. He’d obviously slipped away in a safer, more hidden direction.

I wasn’t surprised. Mule deer get a bad rap for acting dumb during the rut. And it’s true that some bucks seem to throw caution to the wind when love is in the air. But in my experience I’ve seen more evidence of their clever and well-honed survival instincts preserving them from eager hunters, especially when it comes to truly mature bucks.

That afternoon we returned to the base of the ridge. We set up beneath the knob from the previous night because we didn’t want to overcommit and potentially bust the bucks in case they had moved lower down the mountain.

It has been revealed that it wasn’t long before we spotted a fresh buck working its way down a drainage to our right. He was a handsome 4×4 with eyeguards, and Kyle wanted to take him.

Sources indicate that he set his .300 Win. Mag. in a tripod and shot the buck at 350 yards from a kneeling position. The bullet was perfectly placed and the buck ran a few steps and tumbled over. Kyle, Keston, and Kandon (which sounds not unlike a law firm) took off to recover the buck while I stayed behind to keep glassing.

According to recent reports, by the time Keston returned we had about an hour left of shooting light. As luck would have it, we caught sight of the light-colored deer trying to sneak off to the south.

With the pressure we’d applied to the north half of the ridge that morning and afternoon (Kyle’s deer was in the same drainage as the bench where we spotted the buck after first light) I wasn’t surprised to see the older deer trying to put some distance between us and him.

In a recent development, once again it was a race against the falling light. Keston and I took off up the mountain to get within range before dark.

We hiked for 20 minutes to an exposed point that gave us a good view. Keston found the deer again, walking to our left and down toward a thick stand of aspen in a steep draw, where he was about to disappear.

In a recent development, I ranged the deer at 616 yards and got prone, deploying my bipod and setting the butt of the XPR on my shooting bag. The wind, which had been howling earlier in the day, was calming down, but still needed to be accounted for.

I dialed elevation into my scope, held left .4 mil for the wind, and broke the shot. The deer dropped as if poleaxed, kicked a bit, and then lay still. I watched him through my scope with a fresh round chambered until I was sure he was dead.

It has been revealed that by the time we got to the vicinity of the deer it was pitch black. Finding an animal under these conditions can be difficult. And while technology is often a two-edged affairm in this case it was a godsend.

Industry observers note that for the last year, I’ve been using Leupold’s BX-6 rangefinding binocular in shooting competitions and while hunting. I won’t go into all its virtues here, but one feature that’s a game changer is its ability to range a spot and have it drop a pin into a map, like onX Hunt.

That pin led us right to the buck, saving us who knows how much time stumbling around the dark.

Sources indicate that every hunting bullet has the same end goal, which is to inflict massive tissue damage so that the animal swiftly bleeds out, shutting the central nervous system down. (Alternatively, a bullet can strike the CNS directly, with a brain or spinal shot, killing the animal that way.).

How a bullet accomplishes this depends heavily on its construction. Bonded bullets, for instance, are meant to mushroom to a degree, while retaining weight and penetrating deeply.

The BC Max bullet takes a different approach. The large polymer tip on the projectile initiated quick and violent bullet upset. The entrance hole, in the upper portion of the chest, was about two inches across and busted two ribs on the way in.

I could tell the bullet fragmented significantly based on three things: that large entrance wound, the massive tissue damage observed on the deer’s lungs, and the fact that the bullet didn’t penetrate the off side of the ribcage.

We quartered the deer and took backstraps, loins, and neck meat without gutting it, so I didn’t try to recover what was left of the bullet, though I doubt it would have been much.

Recent findings suggest that of all the big mule deer I’ve shot over my career, this one comes closest to the Platonic ideal. He’s a large, clean four-point, with deep, nearly identical, forks front and back, has a tall boxy frame, carries good mass throughout his rack, and has nice eye guards to boot. If one were to draw an idealized symmetrical mule deer, it would look a lot like this one.

I never take an animal like this for granted. He was a wily deer and had given us the slip a couple times already, and was about to make it a third. And, of course, there was his older cousin, that darker, heavier brute, who only highlighted himself once.

We were the last deer hunters on that mountain this season. And my fingers are crossed that the other massive buck, and his kin, make it through the winter.

Sources indicate that I don’t say that because I expect to hunt that spot again. There’s very little chance that will happen. But I do hope some other hunter, who loves these animals the way I do, at least gets to encounter that buck and possibly take him home.

Sources indicate that the best trail running shoes boost our confidence on singletrack to scree fields, sand to slick rock. They’re comfortable and nimble and help us run fast or forever, depending on the adventure. As the days grow shorter and colder we’re also looking for shoes that excel under a wide variety of circumstances, like wet leaves, rime ice, and snow. And as the weather deteriorates, we’re also leaning more on road-to-trail models for the days when the roads and paths are calling our names.

According to recent reports, over two to four months of testing on varied terrain across Santa Barbara to Boulder and Nebraska to New Hampshire, our testers Lisa Jhung, Cory Smith, Johnathan Beverly, and Abby Levene provided detailed feedback on fit, comfort, speed, traction, cushioning, and their joy of running. The result is Trail Runner Magazine’s best trail shoes for fall 2026. Considering that the “best” shoe can run differently on someone else’s feet, our review is specially curated with a shoe claiming the title of each chosen category it achieves best. For even more models, check out Outside’s guide to best trail running shoes for fall.

Weight: 7.5 ounces (men’s 8.5), 6.2 ounces (women’s 8) Stack Height: 28.5–21.5 mm Drop: 7 mm Sizing: 7-12.5, 13, 14, 15 (men’s), 6-11 (women’s).

Pros and Cons + Responsive and springy + Weightless feeling underfoot + Good ground feel + Excellent traction – Runs small (go half a size up) –Expensive.

If the Norda 005 was a car, it would be the Mercedes AMG E63S Wagon. That is to say: it’s quiet performance luxury. IYKYK, as the kids say. Coming in at just 214 grams (7.5 ounces) for a men’s U.S. 8.5, it’s one of the lightest trail running shoes on the market. It’s also made from the highest quality materials: A Biodyneema upper makes it both durable and highly breathable. A slick of Vibram “Megagrip Elite” rubber renders the outsole ultra tacky on the trails while rolling over the roads. And, perhaps most importantly, the midsole is made completely from a proprietary Mouse Arnitel TPEE—a supercritical foam generally only used in small amounts because of the cost—making the shoe featherlight, energetic, and highly durable.

And the simplicity of the design lets the quality shine. As such, it’s a light, fast trail running shoe that can do it all. We’d turn to this shoe for anything from easy days on mixed surfaces, to “fast” trail 100-milers like Western States or Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc. Trail Runner managing editor Abby Levene wore one pair of the Norda 005 for the Tour du Mont Blanc, a five-day, 110-mile adventure through the Alps, and she didn’t think about her feet once. There is no higher praise.

Sources indicate that the midsole is tuned to be slightly firmer than the superfoam in road racers and thus provides an energetic, bouncy ride that doesn’t trampoline you in wild directions off the trail. While the lack of a plate may disqualify the Norda 005 from being a true trail “super shoe,” don’t mistake semantics for inferiority. We didn’t miss a carbon plate here, and its absence allows for enhanced ground feel and adaptability to varied terrain. The foam and rocker deliver a smooth roll and plenty of precision.

It has been revealed that the only real downside to this shoe is the price tag. But sometimes, you get what you pay for. Read our full review of the Norda 005.

Weight: 9.5 oz (men’s), 8.4 oz (women’s) Stack Height: 32–28 mm Drop: 4 mm Sizing: 7-13, 14, 15 (men’s), 5-12 (women’s).

Pros and Cons + Excellent traction + Lightweight and nimble – Slippery laces require double-knotting.

It has been revealed that we’ve tested every version of the Saucony Peregrine since the model’s debut in 2011, and this sixteenth iteration just might be our all-time favorite. The shoe has long been capable of making us feel nimble on rugged terrain, with its great balance of ground feel and cushioning, plus traction on all kinds of trail, wrapped up in a lightweight package. But version 16 takes the Peregrine’s trail capabilities to newly introduced levels, and at $150, it’s an easy pick for Best Value.

The upgraded Vibram Megagrip outsole grips rock slabs with aplomb, while the four-millimeter lugs dig into loose dirt and soft ground (though some sandy-trail testers craved even deeper, toothier lugs). The balanced midsole—not too springy, not too mushy, not too thick—delivers a strong connection to the trail while still feeling responsive and shock absorbing, even during wild descents. The flexible, breathable mesh upper with added toe protection kept out trail debris and warded off snags from roots and branches.

According to recent reports, the fit of this trail running shoe somehow made a variety of testers feel like it was custom-made for them. It locks down the heel, and the just-roomy-enough toebox allowed toe space to breathe while maintaining control. “The fit is just perfect,” mentioned a tester. “I feel secure and supported from heel to toe, and side to side.”.

Weight: 10 oz (men’s), 9 oz (women’s) Stack Height: 33.5 mm–25.5 mm Drop: 8mm Sizing: 7-13, 14 (men’s), 5-11 (women’s).

Pros and Cons + Great traction + Outstanding foothold – Cushioning may feel too firm for some.

The Salomon Genesis 2 earned mountain-goat status among our crew, providing outstanding traction over loose dirt and rock. Its supportive Matryx upper—constructed with thin, high-tenacity yarns and durable Kevlar—secures narrow and wide feet alike via Salomon’s quick-pull lacing system. The forefoot offers slightly more room than version 1, enhancing overall comfort without sacrificing agility.

The outsole, made of Salomon’s Contagrip rubber with toothy, 4 mm lugs, provided excellent traction on all surfaces, giving us confidence, even on scrambles over large rocky slabs and slippery descents.

While the EVA-blend midsole runs firm, it offers direct trail feedback. “This shoe makes it fun to pick a line and charge,” noted one tester. “I felt completely present instead of mindlessly rolling over obstacles.”.

Recent findings suggest that for technical runners who prefer softer cushioning, we also recommend the La Sportiva Prodigio Pro. (Read our full review of the La Sportiva Prodigio Pro here.).

Weight: 11.7 oz (men’s), 9.5 oz (women’s) Stack Height: 39–31 mm Drop: 8 mm Sizing: 6-15 (men’s), 5-12 (women’s).

Pros and Cons + Extremely versatile + Comfortable for all-day wear – Traction could be better.

According to recent reports, the Nike Trail Pegasus 5 has been our top choice for road-to-trail runs for several seasons, so we were concerned that its newly branded replacement, the Nike ACG Pegasus Trail, would mess with its winning formula. But as soon as we stepped into the latest model, we breathed a sigh of relief. The shoe is just as comfortable as its predecessor and, after testing, has proven to be just as capable on and off roads and over gravel, continuing its reign as the most versatile shoe in this roundup.

The midsole foam—Nike’s injection-molded ReactX—feels responsive and cushions comfortably on concrete, pavement, and hard-packed dirt. The outsole traction, from 3.5 mm lugs made of the brand’s proprietary “All Terrain Compound 2.0,” is tackier on wet terrain than the previous version, but still pales in comparison to Vibram MegaGrip.

Sources indicate that what makes this shoe work from roads to singletrack trails is the fit and foothold. Even our most narrow-footed testers felt a secure hold without any pressure points, which allows precise footing on trails, no matter how steep or rocky. This shoe’s versatility makes it a great pick as a one-trick pony for the casual runner who doesn’t need a lighter, faster race shoe, and a solid choice for travel.

Weight: 9.5 oz (unisex) Stack Height: 40–34 mm Drop: 6 mm Sizing: 5-12,13 (men’s), 6.5-13.5, 14.5 (women’s).

Pros and Cons + Extremely lightweight for a 40 mm stack + Great stability – Premium pricetag.

Brooks has a reputation for building a great shoe and sticking to that formula, giving loyal fans a consistent ride, model after model. The tradeoff? It can make the brand seem boring. The all-new Brooks Cascadia Elite shatters that mold. It’s one of the most exciting shoes Brooks has debuted in years, and arguably one of the most exciting trail releases of the year.

Recent findings suggest that despite sharing a name, the Cascadia Elite is nothing like the everyday, cushioned Cascadia trail runner: It’s a trail racing super shoe that is lighter, faster, and more nimble. The standout feature is the 100% PEBA midsole paired with a carbon-infused PEBAX plate that strikes a perfect balance between a springy and stable ride. On smooth, flowy single track in Santa Barbara, CA, running in the Cascadia Elite felt almost effortless, and a ton of fun.

According to recent reports, 40 millimeters under the heel is a lot of foam to deal with, but the ride never felt squishy or overly bouncy in off-camber footing. A wide platform, paired with a flexible, embedded horseshoe-shaped plate, keeps the Cascadia Elite from being tippy. That width does come at a cost, though; picking tight lines through technical terrain requires precise footing to keep from getting wedged between rocks.

If you’re in the market for a trail running shoe, first consider the type of trails you run on regularly: do you tackle rugged, mountainous terrain, or stick to mellow dirt paths? Some trail shoes can handle both adequately, while others are specialized and excel in one or the other. Shoes with smaller lugs are generally better on smoother, firmer terrain, whereas shoes with deeper, more aggressive outsoles are optimized for steep, muddy, or rocky trails. If you like to feel the trail and dance around rocks and roots, you’ll likely prefer a light, more minimal shoe, but if you’d rather let the shoe roll over trail variations, cushioning and protecting while you zone out, you should look for a shoe with a thicker midsole.

Once you’ve narrowed the search to a certain type of trail shoe, you need to find a pair that complements your unique body and stride. Every runner’s body, gait, speed, experience, and ride preferences are different, so every runner will interact differently with each trail shoe. The shoe that your best friend or your sister-in-law loves may be uncomfortable for you and make running feel slow, sluggish, or even painful. Finding the perfect pair of trail running shoes is a seriously personal affair.

The process for choosing the best running shoes is a matter of finding the models that both fit your foot and also feel best when you’re running. To determine fit and feel, there’s no substitute for trying the shoes on and running in them.

When assessing fit, first pay attention to length. You need room at the end of your toes as your feet lengthen during their dynamic movements on the run. A rule of thumb is to allow a thumb’s width between your longest toe and the end of the shoe. Runners often wear a running shoe a half or full size bigger than their street shoes.

Sources indicate that ensure that the shape of the sole and the upper matches your foot shape. The sole should be as wide or wider than your foot for the whole length, and match the curve of your arch comfortably. The shoe should hold your foot securely over the instep, while allowing the ball of the foot and the toes to splay and flex when you roll forward onto them. Your heel shouldn’t slip when you lift it, and the arch should be able to dome and lengthen naturally. Nothing should bind or rub as you roll through the stride.

It has been revealed that if the shoe fits, it’s time to take them on a short run on a treadmill, around the store, or, ideally, down the block and back. Every trail running shoe has a unique ride created by the type and density of foam in the midsole and the geometry of that foam: its thickness, width, heel-to-toe drop, molded sidewalls or flares, and forefoot flexibility or rocker shape (plus, in an increasing number of models, the presence of and type of embedded plate). Each of these elements interact with each other and your stride to determine how the shoe reacts on landing, how much it cushions, how stably it supports, how smoothly it transitions from landing to toe off, and how quickly and powerfully it rebounds.

The best way to choose trail running shoes that complement your body and stride is to find the ones that feel right on the run. Benno Nigg, the world-leading biomechanics professor who proposed this method of shoe selection, calls it the “comfort filter,” but makes clear it is far more than how plush the shoe feels when you step into it. What you want to assess is whether the shoe allows and supports the way your feet want to move, what Nigg calls your “preferred movement path.” In the right shoe, while running at your normal pace, you will touch down where you expect to land, roll smoothly and stably through the stride without noticing the shoe, feel both cushioned from and connected to the ground, and push off naturally, quickly, and powerfully. When this comes together you’ll know that you’ve found your pair.

Recent findings suggest that it’s likely that several shoes will feel good on your feet. To find the most comfortable, it helps to compare them back to back, like an eye doctor will do with corrective lenses: flipping between “A” or “B,” “1” or “2.” You may also find that different shoes feel better at different paces or level of fatigue, and you may want more than one pair. In fact, research indicates that wearing a variety of different shoes is one of the few proven ways to reduce injury risk as it appears to vary the stresses on your feet and joints.

In a recent development, running shoes have long been marketed and sold as prescriptive devices to help runners stay healthy, but there is little scientific evidence correlating shoes, or any specific shoe properties—like cushioning or pronation control—with running injuries. Medical professionals say that it is highly difficult to determine whether a runner needs a certain type of shoe, and studies have shown that prescribing shoes using traditional methods like treadmill gait analyses or wet-foot arch height tests don’t consistently reduce injuries.

Don’t assume that you need more cushioning or more stability if you have sore joints, or if you’re a heavier runner, or if you’re a beginner—evidence doesn’t support many common beliefs. The best way prevent injury is find two or three different pairs that feel right on the run, ease into using them, and vary your shoes, your running surface and your pace regularly (plus avoid rapid increases in your training load and work on improving your mechanics).

Each season, we evaluate new releases from top outdoor brands, distributing samples to testers based on foot shape and local trail conditions and preferences. For this fall enhancement, we evaluated 5 new models alongside 91 previously tested shoes to select the best trail running shoes on the market.

Over two to four months of testing on varied terrain across the country (from Santa Barbara to Boulder, Nebraska to Fresh Hampshire), our team provided detailed feedback on fit, comfort, traction, cushioning, and responsiveness. We combined these reports with our own trail testing to select category winners and top recommendations for every type of runner.

It has been revealed that freelance journalist, editor, and author Lisa Jhung has researched, tested, and written about running shoes for the past decade and a half, much of that time for Outside. She coordinates a fleet of female shoe testers out of Boulder, Colorado, and notes her home office is a perpetual obstacle course of cardboard boxes and piles of running shoes. Lisa’s written about gear of all kinds for numerous national magazines as both an editor and freelancer, including a stint as the shoes and gear blogger and trail running microsite editor for Runner’s World.

A high school jumper and occasional sprinter/hurdler, she started running—really running—after walking off the collegiate volleyball team, and moved on to road and trail races of any distance, triathlons, adventure races, and mountain running. She’s happiest testing rugged trail shoes on gnarly terrain, and also loves a good neighborhood jaunt…but is almost always looking for ribbons of dirt. Lisa is the author of Running That Doesn’t Suck: How to Love Running (Even if You Think You Hate It) and Trailhead: The Dirt on All Things Trail Running.

Cory’s passion for running started over 30 years ago in high school when he became the number six ranked runner in the nation at 3000 meters his senior year. After high school, he competed at Villanova University, earning two NCAA Division I Championship showings. Today, he’s determined not to let age slow him down and competes on the national master’s circuit, running a 4:12 (4:30 mile pace) 1500 meters and 9:04 (4:52 mile pace) 3000 meters in 2021 at age 43. He prefers a hard track workout or tempo run over an easy long run any day but also appreciates a challenging trail or mountain run.

It has been revealed that his obsession with running shoes started in 2014 when he wrote his first shoe review for Gear Institute. Since then, he’s tested and reviewed hundreds of running shoes, clothing, and gear for Outside, Runner’s World, Footwear News, and other outlets. He has a soft spot for speedy shoes over heavy trainers but loves dissecting all shoes equally and thinking like a product engineer to explain the why behind every design detail. Cory is the Founder of Run Your Personal Best, an online running coaching business, and since its inception in 2014, has coached runners to over 100 Boston Marathon Qualifying times.

One of Cory Smith’s go-to routes for testing trail running shoes:.

Jonathan fell in love with running his freshman year of high school and rapidly became fascinated with finding the perfect pair of running shoes. That quest got a boost when he became editor of Running Times in 2000 and started receiving every upcoming model as they were released. The parade of shoes continued while he served as shoe editor for Runner’s World, then editor of PodiumRunner, and currently fitness gear editor at Outside. Having now worn nearly every running shoe created in this century—and a fair amount of those dating back to the early models of the ’70s—he’s given up on finding the one best and now relishes the wide variety of excellent options.

In a recent development, once a 2:46 marathoner regularly doing 50+ mile weeks, recent injuries and his age have reduced his volume and slowed his pace—but he still enjoys an uptempo workout or two each week. Beverly is the author of the book Your Best Stride which explores how each individual’s gait—and thus shoe preference—is unique. He enjoys getting scientists’ take on latest shoe trends and trying to describe the nuances of each shoe’s ride.

#56356. Two Borrowed Shotguns, Two Record Bucks, and the Best Opening Morning in Ohio History

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3687 w)

Two Borrowed Shotguns, Two Record Bucks, and the Best Opening Morning in Ohio History

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3687 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This story, “The Luck of Irish Ridge,” appeared in the December 1966 issue of Outdoor Life.
  • According to recent reports, the 1965 deer season in the hill country of southeastern Ohio was 15 minutes old, but the woods were silent.
  • But I didn’t want to risk moving, now that shooting was legal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story, “The Luck of Irish Ridge,” appeared in the December 1966 issue of Outdoor Life. While it was an incredible deer, Ohio is an incredible state for substantial whitetails. Allison’s buck is now ranked 41 among Ohio’s biggest typical bucks.

According to recent reports, the 1965 deer season in the hill country of southeastern Ohio was 15 minutes old, but the woods were silent. I was hunkered down with my back against a tree in an open place on the side of a big ridge. The place was too open, but I hadn’t realized that when I sat down there just before the opening hour of 9 o’clock. A deer could see me a mile away, I told myself.

But I didn’t want to risk moving, now that shooting was legal. Anyway, I didn’t know where there was a better stand. So I just sat still, hoping for the best.

It was a clear November morning, frosty but promising to warm up later. Most of the timber on the side of the ridge was oak. That meant acorns, and acorns are likely to mean deer. Maybe I hadn’t picked such a bad spot after all. It was warm and pleasant there in the sun. I’d wait awhile and see what happened.

Industry observers note that suddenly, the stillness was shattered by a shot. A few seconds later another one rapped out. Though I wasn’t sure which direction the shots came from, I decided it was some hunter over the ridge behind me. I didn’t dream what had happened. The woods got quiet again, and then bluejays started to holler on the ridge.

According to recent reports, I’d hunted deer only three years before this and was too inexperienced to know what those noisy bluejays meant. I’ll know next time.

Recent findings suggest that the next thing I heard was something moving in the dry oak leaves behind me. It didn’t sound major enough for a deer, but it startled me. I swiveled my head slowly for a look. It seemed to take me an eternity to turn my head and body without making any sudden motions or noise.

Industry observers note that whatever I was hearing kept coming, walking slowly and deliberately. I finally got twisted into position and eased one eye around the trunk of the tree I’d been sitting against.

What I saw then literally took my breath away.

Walking slowly down the slope, only 15 or 20 yards away and coming almost straight toward me, was a giant buck with the biggest rack I’d ever seen. The morning sun glinted on his polished, brown tines, and he looked as if he were wearing the bleached roots of an upturned stump on his head. I didn’t know it then, but I was looking at a whitetail deer that was better than any that had ever been killed in Ohio.

According to recent reports, he stopped for a second and looked back up the ridge, the direction he’d come from, and I remember thinking that somebody over there must have spooked him. Then he turned my way and came on, walking calmly and unafraid. To this day, I don’t know why I didn’t have the worst case of buck fever a young deer hunter ever had.

In a recent development, my dad, Don Allison, and I had left home the previous evening and driven to Wellston, where we were to stay for the hunting season with dad’s friend and hunting partner, Jim Arthur. We live near South Solon, in the flat prairie country about 40 miles southwest of Columbus. Dad runs a 232-acre farm on some of the nation’s richest land. He handles a herd of 20 Black Angus cows and their calves and feeds out about 350 hogs a year.

I was 17 years old at the time and a senior at Madison South High School south of London.

I’ve hunted with dad ever since I could carry a gun. We get rabbits, pheasants, and fox squirrels in the farming areas around home, and the last few years we’ve made trips for grouse to the hill country of eastern Ohio. In 1962, dad took me deer hunting for the first time.

Recent findings suggest that the deer season is the only real vacation dad takes. He started hunting deer in 1944, the second year Ohio had an open season, and has missed only one fall since, except for years when the season was closed. But he’s been plagued by hard luck. In almost 20 years of hunting, up to last fall, he’d never killed a deer.

Recent findings suggest that the closest he ever came was getting a shot at a doe, but he confessed that buck fever — if a female deer can give you buck fever — got the best of him that time, and he scored a clean miss. He loves to hunt, though, and has never gotten discouraged.

“I’ll be lucky one of these years,” he always mentioned, not knowing just how lucky.

Industry observers note that my record was no better. In three falls of hunting, I hadn’t even seen a deer. But, like dad, I was sure my time would come.

In a recent development, ohio’s 1965 gun season on deer was a restricted one, varying from region to region according to herd conditions and the management intends of the state game men. In the northwestern counties, level farm country, there was a three-day either-sex season, but hunters had to have in advance a landowner’s written permission to hunt in order to get a deer permit.

In the hill country of southeastern Ohio, where we’ve always hunted, there was a bucks-only season beginning on Monday, November 8, and lasting four days. Hunting hours were from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., and only shotguns loaded with slugs or pumpkin balls were legal, as in the past.

As November drew near, dad and I both developed the usual deer-hunting itch. It’s hard to tell anybody how much our annual whitetail hunt means to us. But for a time, it didn’t look as if either of us could make it. Dad had almost 100 acres of corn to pick. Deer season was about a month earlier than usual, and the picking job would be no more than well started by November 8. If he took time off to go hunting, wintry weather could set in before he finished the corn picking.

“I’m going,” he finally told us, “even if I have to pick corn when the snow’s blowing.”.

In a recent development, my problem was basketball — I had a good chance to make the school team. We’d practiced about a week when deer season rolled around, and the rule was that anybody who missed practice unexcused would be dropped from the squad.

It was a fair rule, and I knew going deer hunting wasn’t a valid excuse. If I went, my basketball career would end before it started. But the hunt was too much to pass up.

“If you’re going,” I told dad, “so am I.”.

There was one other problem. We both had gun trouble. Dad usually shoots a Model 12 Winchester 12 gauge that he’s had for years. But it was out of order, so he borrowed a 12 gauge Remington autoloader. I was getting ready to buy a new shotgun, so I borrowed a Browning 16 gauge automatic on trial. We’d both be using guns we’d had little chance to get familiar with.

“Well, if we see deer and miss,” dad mentioned with a grin, “at least we’ve got a good alibi.”.

Industry observers note that dad hunted for many years in the Shawnee State Forest, along the Ohio River west of Portsmouth. It’s a 60,000-acre tract, rugged and steep, with oak-covered ridges and few roads. It’s easy to get lost there unless you’re familiar with the hills. Other parts of Ohio may have more deer, but many hunters prefer this wild country.

Dad had another reason for hunting there. It was the favorite spot of a good friend of his, Belvin Adams. Adams lived in Wheelersburg, only a short distance away, and he and a party of his friends had hunted the Shawnee for years.

In a recent development, but three years ago, the rubber firm Adams works for moved him to Indonesia. Since then, Jim Arthur, who lives in Wellston and had worked with Adams, has invited dad and me to stay at his home and hunt with his party in the Raccoon and Zaleski state forests, in Vinton County. These forests have a combined area of about 30,000 acres, and the timberlands are mixed with some farming acreage, making good deer range. That was where dad and I would go for the 1965 season.

Jim Arthur has a son, Steve, who’s my age and, like me, was a senior in high school then. We have a lot in common, especially our enthusiasm for deer hunting.

Industry observers note that we got to Wellston Sunday evening, too late to scout the area we intended to hunt. And Jim Arthur told us that he’d been too busy to do any looking in recent weeks. That meant we’d start cold on opening day, not knowing where deer were hanging out or where their feeding grounds and travel routes were. But at least we’d hunted the general area for three years and knew the lay of the land.

According to recent reports, we sat up late that night, as we usually do the night before the season opens, recalling other hunts, laying plans, guessing what kind of luck we’d have. And the longer we talked, the higher our hunting fever mounted.

According to recent reports, we turned in finally, got a few hours of sleep, and were up early, checking our equipment and taking care of last-minute details. About 8 o’clock, though we couldn’t start hunting for another hour, we drove out to a long hogback called Irish Ridge, between the Raccoon and Little Raccoon creeks, a few miles southeast of Wellston. We didn’t want another party to beat us to our stands, and we wanted to be set at 9 o’clock in case hunters around us began moving deer.

I followed an abandoned township road that wound along the side of the ridge. Steve was quite a way below me on the slope, his dad was walking the crest of the ridge, and my dad was about halfway down on the other side. A few minutes before 9, I picked the oak-tree stand I described in the beginning and settled down.

Industry observers note that I heard the two shots and heard the bluejays yell. Then that huge buck came walking slowly down the ridge.

Industry observers note that I eased into shooting position slowly and carefully, and I raised the Browning just as cautiously. The buck took a few more steps, reached the old, leaf-strewn road, and stopped to look around. He was only 30 feet away. I had time to remind myself that I was using an unfamiliar gun and to remember how it worked. I pushed the safety off and leveled on him.

Dad had told me many times to shoot for the spine when my chance came. I remembered that advice now and followed it. My 16 gauge rifled slug smashed through the deer’s backbone just behind the shoulders, and he fell like a ton of bricks. But he pulled himself half up on his forelegs, so I did the second thing dad had always instructed me to do.

“Once you get a deer down,” he’d said, “shoot for the heart and finish him in a hurry.”.

Recent findings suggest that dad had read a lot about deer hunting and talked with many hunters, and it never occurred to me that there was anything strange about his having such firm opinions, even though he’d never killed a deer. His advice proved itself again now. I put in a heart shot, and this time the buck didn’t get up.

Sources indicate that he was still thrashing around, though, working himself downhill. And suddenly I saw that he was going to fall over a low cliff. I watched, and my heart sank as he rolled over the edge and disappeared. The cliff muffled his fall, and I ran to the edge, almost afraid to look. If part of that magnificent rack had broken, I’d be sick.

Sources indicate that he lay dead at the foot of the cliff, 20 or 30 feet below. One front leg, broken in the fall, stuck out at an angle. I couldn’t see enough of his horns to tell about them.

I waited long enough to be sure he was dead and then found a place where I could climb down. I took a good look at his head and breathed a gusty sigh of relief. Not a single point was damaged. Was I thankful!

After my heart stopped thumping, I started wondering how we’d ever get him up to the old road. We couldn’t take him up the cliff, and there was a very steep grade wherever I looked. But before I had time to think much, I heard Steve call. I yelled back, and in a few minutes he joined me. When he saw what I’d shot, he was about as excited as I was, and I guess I was as proud as anybody in Ohio right then.

In a recent development, I had never dressed a deer, so I asked Steve to stay with the buck while I went to find dad. I climbed to the top of the ridge and, before going much farther, heard voices down in a brushy gully. I shouted.

“Come on down,” dad remarked. When I got there, he and Jim were standing over a mighty major buck, and dad had the happiest look on his face that I’d ever seen.

He had killed his deer almost exactly as I’d taken mine and not more than five minutes earlier. The two shots I’d heard were his.

He’d walked in along the side of the ridge and found the kind of stand he was looking for. He was about to sit when he heard something rustling the dry leaves behind him. When he turned around, there came a big buck, walking downhill toward him.

The deer didn’t see him, and dad waited until it was abreast of him and only 40 feet away. Then he floored it with a spine shot. After falling, it slid down into a gully and out of sight. Dad ran up to the edge and saw that the deer was still kicking, so he finished it off with a slug through the heart.

“I got one the same way over on the other side of the ridge,” I blurted out. Then I took another look at dad’s buck and added, “Only mine’s bigger.”.

We shook hands and thumped each other on the back, and I don’t believe there were ever two happier hunters in the deer woods. After 20 years of waiting and trying for dad, and four for me, it was hard to believe that we’d killed two bucks, both massive busters, in the first half hour of the season, within a few hundred yards of each other, and with borrowed guns. What luck!

It has been revealed that as far as we’ve been able to find out, we were the first father-and-son team ever to take two record-book trophies — both of our bucks turned out to be that — in a single season anywhere in the country, to say nothing of getting them in such a hurry. Those certainly were 20 magic minutes.

Sources indicate that jim and dad had been trying to figure out a way to hang dad’s buck. With three pairs of hands to hoist and heave, it wasn’t too hard. As soon as it was done, Jim started back with me to dress my deer while dad went to work on his.

Sources indicate that we found we couldn’t hang my buck. The slope was too steep, and there were no suitable trees. But Jim, Steve, and I pulled and skidded it around so that the head was uphill. Then Jim demonstrated me how to field-dress a deer where it lay.

It has been revealed that four other men, friends of Jim’s and dad’s, had started out to hunt with us that morning. Three of them were nearby, heard us yelling, and came to help. We needed them. Even with part of the crew pulling on ropes and the rest lifting and pushing, it was all the seven of us could do to get my buck up the slope to the old road.

We left him there, went after dad’s, and skidded it to the ridge top. Then we dragged the two bucks out to the cars. It was past noon when we finished and headed to town for lunch.

We hung our two deer side by side in Jim Arthur’s yard. Cars drove by in a steady stream the rest of the day as word of our trophies got around Wellston. Dad phoned home, and mother and Joan Mace, wife of a neighboring farmer, agreed to drive down in the Mace pickup and take the deer home.

Sources indicate that by the time they got to the Arthur home, there was so much traffic around it that they had to park two blocks away. We cleared a path through the traffic, loaded the deer, and drove back to the state checking station for the required check.

It has been revealed that the bucks were weighed the next morning. Field-dressed, with heart and lungs out, mine tallied 253 pounds, dad’s 240. According to the conversion table we used to estimate their live weight, mine would have gone just over 300 when I shot it, dad’s almost 290.

It has been revealed that we took the heads to Max Shipley, a Columbus taxidermist. The minute he saw them, he phoned Merrill Gilfillan of the Ohio Division of Wildlife, to whom I have related this story. Merrill is an official scorer for both the Buckeye Major Bucks Club and the Boone and Crockett Club.

Both were typical-whitetail racks, and to our delight both made the record lists of both clubs. After the required 60-day shrinkage period, mine scored a whopping 187 6/8, dad’s 160 2/8. Up until this point, we hadn’t realized how significant our bucks really were.

Recent findings suggest that according to the 1964 edition of the Boone and Crockett Club’s Records of North American Big Game, mine is the biggest typical whitetail ever killed in Ohio and rates a place among the first 10 on the list. I have entered it in the 1966-67 Boone and Crockett competition. Officials tell me that any deer scoring that high has a very good chance of winning first place among typical whitetails in that competition.

It has been revealed that for some reason, Ohio produces far more than its fair share of big whitetail heads. It’s by no means one of the big deer-kill states. The herd numbers only an estimated 20,000 to 30,000, and in recent years hunters have killed fewer than 1,000 annually, as compared with kills of 100,000 and more in such leading whitetail states as Minnesota, Michigan, and Wisconsin.

In a recent development, yet there has been no recent season that did not see three to five Ohio bucks make the Boone and Crockett record list in either the typical or nontypical category. In six open seasons between 1956 and 1962 (deer hunting was closed in 1961), 24 Ohio deer qualified for that honor, 13 of them typical racks, 11 nontypical.

We shook hands and thumped each other on the back, and I don’t believe there were ever two happier hunters in the deer woods.

And in the 1958-59 substantial-game competition sponsored by the Boone and Crockett Club, Ohio whitetails — one with a typical rack and the other nontypical — won first place in both those categories.

The nontypical deer was killed in Ashtabula County in 1957 by James L. Clark of Ashtabula, and the typical buck in Harrison County a year later. Dr. James Rumbaugh and John Ruyan of Westerville shared the honors on that one, both having shot at it. Clark, in collaboration with Merrill Gilfillan, told the story of those two busters in “How I Got No. 1 Deer,” in the November, 1960, matter of Outdoor Life.

In addition, about 180 heads have qualified in the last 10 years for a place on the record list of the Buckeye Big Bucks Club, a state organization sponsored by the Division of Wildlife. Minimum score requirement for this club is 140, just 20 points below that of the Boone and Crockett Club.

In a recent development, game men believe that Ohio’s phenomenal showing is due to a favorable combination of cropland and woodland — providing an abundance of top-quality deer food — plus certain trace minerals in the soil and hunting rules that have prevented both overhunting and overcrowding of the range. Vinton County, for example, where we hunted, is more than two thirds woods and brush but does have some farmland, including cornfields, in the valleys. That’s likely to mean big, healthy deer.

Read Next: The Incredible Hunt for the C.W. Shelton Buck, One of the Widest Bucks in the World.

In a recent development, as for the consequences of our hunt, dad fared better than I did. He finished his corn picking in cold weather but without any real problems. But I missed out on something pretty special. Our basketball team turned out to be a championship outfit, winning the Darby Valley League pennant and all but the last game in the district tournament. But I wasn’t on it.

Dad and I were both disappointed about that, but if I were doing it over again, I’d make the same choice. I can’t ever be sorry I went on that deer hunt.

#56355. Public-Land Sales, Energy Dominance, and Data Centers: What Interior’s Master Blueprint Really Means for Outdoorsmen
