In a recent development, outside+ members can enjoy exclusive Ski Perks discounts on ski gear, apparel, rentals, and more from top outdoor brands. (Photo: Keri Bascetta).

We skiers love a good deal, especially on gear. And if you’ve ever wished you had access to the kinds of discounts usually reserved for ski industry insiders, here’s something worth knowing about.

Outside+ members now have access to Ski Perks, a collection of exclusive discounts and offers from ski and outdoor brands, included with their membership at no additional cost. We’re talking savings on everything from ski apparel and accessories to equipment rentals and recovery tools.

Outside+ already gives you access to an impressive collection of outdoor stories and resources, from gear reviews and adventure films to GPS apps that help you plan your next adventure outdoors. Our goal is to give you best-in-class content and the tools to help you get outside more often and make the most of it.

For skiers, that means unlimited gear reviews, destination guides, and expert advice from SKI, plus original reporting from publications like Outside, Backpacker, RUN, and more. Eligible U.S. members will also receive a print subscription to Outside magazine. Stream Warren Miller films and other adventure programming on Outside TV, explore trails with Trailforks Pro, track your activities with MapMyFitness, and proposal your next adventure with Gaia GPS Premium.

And now, you’ve got another way to put that membership to good use.

The lineup includes offers on everything from outerwear and accessories to rentals, recovery gear, and premium weather forecasts. Here’s what’s available:.

Check back throughout the ski season for even more perks coming soon.

In a recent development, not a member yet? Join Outside+ here to unlock Ski Perks and everything else that comes with your membership.

So, the next time you’ve got your eye on a latest jacket from our Winter Gear Guide, need to replace your gloves, or are planning a ski trip to one of the Top 50 Resorts in North America, check your Ski Perks before you pull out your credit card. You might find a pretty good deal waiting for you.

#56307. Tech Report: The Glacier Died—And the Trail Runners Started Coming

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2702 w)

Tech Report: The Glacier Died—And the Trail Runners Started Coming

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2702 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’m standing with Samuel Mendoza on top of Chacaltaya Mountain, 17,785 feet above sea level.
  • Directly ahead, the Altiplano—the high plain—stretches from the foot of the mountain.
  • Behind us rises the Huayna Potosí massif.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’m standing with Samuel Mendoza on top of Chacaltaya Mountain, 17,785 feet above sea level. Under our feet is a sharp slope of scree, a jumbled descent of rocks with patches of snow. The air is thin, and the vast Bolivian landscape surrounds us.

Directly ahead, the Altiplano—the high plain—stretches from the foot of the mountain. El Alto, the chaotic concrete and red brick city that has grown to roughly 900,000 people, lies at the far edge of the plain at 13,000 feet of elevation, crammed against a canyon’s edge. About 1,500 feet below and connected by a series of cable cars, La Paz, Bolivia’s seat of government, sprawls.

Behind us rises the Huayna Potosí massif. The nearly 20,000-foot summit towers above, its glaciated peak passing in and out of fast-moving clouds. About 45 miles to the northwest, Lake Titicaca—the central motif to Inca creation stories—shimmers on the horizon.

It’s here, on this high mountain of almost-bare rock cradled in the Andes, that Mendoza learned to ski.

According to recent reports, located roughly 20 miles north of La Paz, Chacaltaya was once the world’s highest-altitude ski resort. It began in the 1930s when Raúl Posnansky, an engineer and ski enthusiast, recognized the mountain’s potential, according to 2023 reporting by “Radio Ambulante.” Chacaltaya’s glacier, though relatively small in area at roughly 55 acres, was a solid tongue of ice descending the slope. Temperatures up high stayed low, and snow fell heavily and often during the wet season. The ice was there, had always been there, and would always be there, by all indications at the time.

Posnansky worked to materialize his skiing fantasy: He hired laborers to build an access road, haul materials, construct cabins, and install the first rope tow at Chacaltaya—powered by a truck engine housed in a cabin hanging over the base of the ski run.

It has been revealed that posnansky, along with other mountain athletes, founded the Club Andino Boliviano, a group of dedicated skiers and enthusiasts. To fund the growing ski scene, the club drew involvement from La Paz’s middle and upper classes, and Posnansky and the club persuaded Bolivia’s Congress to pass tax legislation dedicating 1% of the country’s hotel revenue to Bolivia’s Ski and Mountaineering Federation. This funding would help transform Chacaltaya from a passion project into the hub of Bolivian skiing—a hub that, while retaining its roughshod, backyard roots, would grow to host a national ski team, crowded weekend races, the first South American ski championships, and athletes who would represent the country at Winter Olympics.

When Mendoza was a young boy in El Alto, his family wasn’t connected to La Paz’s urban elite who would drive across the Altiplano to ski. Mendoza’s father, however, worked as the caretaker of Chacaltaya, often living for weeks at a time at the resort to maintain the facilities.

Industry observers note that when he was 15, Mendoza accompanied his father to the mountain for the first time. He spent his first night at the base racked by altitude sickness.

Recent findings suggest that “My dad gave me coca leaf tea,” he says. The next day, “the sun came out; I felt better. I got acclimated, and I learned to ski.”.

Fifty years later, standing once again on the summit, Mendoza is transported back to the resort’s heyday.

Recent findings suggest that “The rope would drop us off here,” he says. “And then …” He puts his hands on bent knees and waves them back and forth in a slalom. He raises his hands over his head and lets out a high yell, feeling the old rush of racing in the cold air.

In a recent development, mendoza is in his 60s now. He has a harder time seeing, looking out through thick glasses, and his knees sometimes bother him.

Around us the glacier has completely vanished, leaving behind only a mountain of rock.

It has been revealed that infatuated with the world of snow and slopes, Mendoza learned to ski on gear borrowed from Club Andino. He worked long, physical days with his father, tasks ranging from construction and upkeep to manning the rope tow—including rebraiding the wire cable whenever it snapped, a job that left Mendoza with thin white scars across his fingers. From his father, he learned to manage the mountain, the two often sleeping in the lodge for weeks at a time.

Meanwhile, his love for skiing only deepened. Mendoza remembers Stanley Shepard, an American diplomat posted in Bolivia, who taught him advanced techniques and shared the joy of the mountain.

“Stan would drive up this road so fast,” he says as we drive the same route from the city to Chacaltaya some 50 years later. He smiles with the memory of the adrenaline rush.

In a recent development, mendoza’s ski story exists in a split reality: In one, he is the caretaker’s son, surrounded by a country’s elites who lived near, but not next to, families like his. The socioeconomic divide paralleled the geography: La Paz’s wealthy neighborhoods in the valley, El Alto on the cold outcropping of the Altiplano above. Despite the divide, Mendoza was a vital member of the Chacaltaya scene; the members of Club Andino were his friends. The nights were full of music whenever others would sleep alongside him and his father at the refugio. The period is marked in Mendoza’s mind by shared meals in the cabin and shared runs on the mountain.

Recent findings suggest that by the 1970s, with Chacaltaya entering its golden period, Mendoza was both employee and skier. He tells me he used to set up for the weekend slalom races—ones he’d often compete in as well. I ask about the slalom poles, curious about infrastructure. He tells me they were made nearby. “But the first times,” he indicates, “we used hollow canes, like cornstalks.”.

According to recent reports, in a 1976 article in Ski Magazine, American writer Jeff Frees described his visit to the ski hill. There were some two dozen weekly skiers sharing the piste and “a slightly doglegged swath of snow” that was “lined with rocks from top to bottom,” although there were no lift lines, he writes.

According to recent reports, the chalet, perched on a rocky precipice, was “so frightening and insecure-looking,” that “some skiers refused to enter it,” Frees says. With the altitude nearing 18,000 feet, other visitors didn’t even bother trying, exiting the minibus up from La Paz only to climb into the truck heading back down the road.

This was the electric, eclectic golden period. One 1,000-foot run served by a single rope tow prone to snapping and powered by a truck engine. A handful of foreign visitors and the dedicated group of Club Andino members. A small, warm refugio built on a cliffside, filled with coca tea, quinoa soup, and music. Weekend races and training events for young locals, supporting ski teams who would go on to participate in four consecutive Olympics starting in 1980. And behind this incredible scene was Samuel Mendoza.

Sources indicate that “It was frozen all the time,” Mendoza says. “The people stated, ‘This is forever. It will never recede.’”.

“But little by little, it started to thaw.”.

Scientists had been documenting Chacaltaya for decades, but a systematic study of the glacier began in 1991, led in part by Edson Ramírez of the Universidad Mayor de San Andrés in La Paz (UMSA). Glaciologists’ observations began to echo the concerns skiers had voiced for years: Chacaltaya was melting—and fast.

“Snow would fall at night,” Mendoza says, “but it would be gone by midday.” As temperatures rose, the glacier retreated, exposing more and more of the rock underneath.

While the retreat was evident in some of the earliest photos from the 1940s, Ramírez and his team found that, in just six years from 1992 to 1998, the glacier’s melt had accelerated dramatically, losing more than 40% of its surface area and roughly two-thirds of its ice volume. The team’s prediction: The glacier would disappear within 10 to 15 years.

By 2009, the glacier was completely gone.

“The entire glacier of the world’s highest ski slope had turned to water,” Mendoza reflects.

Recent findings suggest that as the ski run melted under them, various last-ditch efforts were implemented to keep the sport alive. Artificial snow production was attempted, but ultimately proved too costly. Moving the resort to other nearby mountains was considered, but transportation and access were constant hurdles. Even traditional Andean rituals were offered to the mountain gods.

But the glacier, once gone, would not come back.

Without their ski hub, the Club Andino eventually unraveled. A photo hangs in the abandoned refugio of smiling members piled outside the club. Mendoza tells me their names—a running list of friends moved abroad or passed away. Even their headquarters in La Paz is now shuttered.

Sources indicate that while sooner than expected, Chacaltaya’s glacier death was not unique within the broader scope of Andean glaciers. Research published in 2026 by Giuliana Adrianzen and Andrew Malone of the University of Illinois Chicago found that Bolivia’s Cordillera Real lost a stunning 42% of its glaciated area between 1992 and 2024.

This trend is widespread across the Andes, which are home to 99% of the world’s tropical glacier area—particularly vulnerable ice fields located near the Earth’s equator.

Glaciers in this latitudinal band are much more susceptible to small temperature changes than those outside of it. Kept frozen primarily by extreme altitude, tropical glaciers already exist close to the temperature threshold to sustain permanent ice; they also don’t experience the long, cold winters of glaciers nearer the poles. Andean glaciers are now thinning 35% faster than the global average, according to a 2025 international report co-authored by researchers at the University of Sheffield. As global warming pushes the freezing level higher, more precipitation falls on these glaciers as rain instead of snow, accelerating the melt.

Over the 60 years between 1960 and 2020, Peru lost 56% of its glacier area. In 2024, Venezuela was declared glacier-free with the death of the Humboldt Glacier (named, perhaps ominously, after the German naturalist who pioneered the notion that everything in the natural world is connected). Colombia is following the same trajectory, having lost more than 90% of its glaciated area since the mid-1800s.

According to UNESCO, the Andes could lose 78 to 97% of their tropical glacier volume by the year 2100.

According to recent reports, of course, more than skiing is at risk—including the water supply risk of some 90 million people across the Andes. These glaciers serve as water reserves for the millions of people who live downstream, and their disappearance foreshadows looming ecological disasters. Many Andean municipalities also rely on hydroelectric power, which depends on steady dry-season meltwater from the glaciers. As the glaciers shrink, that flow is dwindling, increasing the severity of droughts.

Sources indicate that while Chacaltaya’s lift has long since stopped spinning, a handful of trained guides and foreign clients continue to practice ski mountaineering in Bolivia, climbing high peaks and bombing descents on still-intact glaciers. While the chalet has ceased to function, the mountain remains an active scientific base. The Chacaltaya Observatory, run by UMSA’s Laboratory for Atmospheric Physics—with multiple international collaborators—continues to measure the atmosphere, climate, and cosmic rays.

And although skiing has abandoned the mountain, Mendoza has not.

Sources indicate that since his father died on Chacaltaya over 30 years ago, Mendoza has served as the mountain’s main caretaker, a position he continues to hold. He spends more time in El Alto with his family now, but he and his brother Adolfo still make multiple trips a week to Chacaltaya, welcoming the handful of tourists who come to visit the abandoned chalet or use it as an acclimatization hike. With the small collected entrance fees, he pays for repairs and maintains his memories of the resort.

Many of Mendoza’s days, however, are spent in solitude, standing alone at 17,000 feet on Chacaltaya’s rocky remains.

According to recent reports, “When you’re alone it’s a little sad,” he claims. “With only the birds, the condors, the Andean foxes.”.

Since the collapse of the glacier, a upcoming group of athletes has taken to Chacaltaya: trail runners—whose arrival is directly tied to skiing’s disappearance. Paolo Choque is the director of skyrunning for the Bolivian Ski and Mountaineering Federation. One of the “last people to learn to ski in Bolivia,” Choque witnessed the collapse of skiing at Chacaltaya, and he has since helped cultivate trail running to take its place.

In 2001, when Choque learned to ski, the main chunk of the glacier was already “ruined,” he says. Against the backdrop of the dying mountain, Choque became involved in promoting skiing and snowboarding in Bolivia, including searching for alternative mountains to host competitions.

Recent findings suggest that in 2011, the federation found another suitable slope at nearby Charquini and hosted a Bolivian Ski Championship. Choque claims that snowboarding grew in popularity over a handful of years with the promotion efforts, but participation numbers remained low—with just 25 racers in the snowboard event in 2015. Amid melting ice and low participation, he made the decision to pivot. “I said, ‘No, this isn’t going anywhere. We don’t even have a ski slope.’”.

According to recent reports, inspired by the sport’s explosion in Spain, Choque organized a pilot skyrunning race on Chacaltaya in 2016, which was met with a strong reception. Athletes had returned to the mountain. The federation’s championship now draws about 200 participants each year, according to Choque. Racers gain points at multiple events across the country, which take place over otherworldly terrain—from the world’s largest salt flats in Uyuni to the folds of the Sajama stratovolcano, the shores of Lake Titicaca, and, of course, Chacaltaya Mountain.

“Skiing may have died,” Choque claims, “but mountain sports have not.”.

In a recent development, while private trail races have also increased in popularity in Bolivia over the past decade, the federation aims to develop skyrunning and its next generation of athletes through accessible competition. Race entries, Choque emphasizes, are kept inexpensive, and youth competition categories give athletes the opportunity to qualify for international competition.

“For me, sport must come first, and it must be accessible to everyone,” Choque says.

Despite challenges with funding, Choque says the federation has seen success in sending participants to compete in the South American Championships, where they have earned podium finishes, including three medals in 2025.

As one sport fades and another grows, Choque defines what success could look like for Bolivian skyrunning.

Sources indicate that “What I want to achieve is to bring a South American championship here, and if possible, even a youth world championship to Bolivia,” he says. “We have the potential.”.

Paolo and the federation hope that Chacaltaya will continue to be an vital mountain hub for decades to come—with or without the glacier.

For all of the uniqueness of Chacaltaya’s history, it does mirror a larger global skiing trend: most of the participants were wealthy. Mendoza remembers well the divide caused by the cost of equipment. “From the city of El Alto there weren’t a lot of skiers,” he notes.

In a recent development, through the Ski and Mountaineering Federation, Choque is determined that the next iteration of Chacaltaya’s mountain sports—trail and sky running—do not follow the same pattern. Mendoza, meanwhile, has seen some of the runners who are taking to the mountain to train where he once skied. I ask him if he would ever run one of the races, and he tells me he enjoys running. His knees, though, keep him from doing too much of it. But when a German tourist wanted to race from the summit to the lagoon below, Mendoza happily noted yes.

“Replacing skiing at Chacaltaya in the future is possible,” he says.

Looking across the dry slope where he learned to ski, the rusted remains of his rope tow, the faded chalet and the memories contained, Mendoza takes a deep breath. At the end of the day, as we drive the winding dirt road down to the city with Chacaltaya shrinking into the distance behind us, he looks ahead.

“It makes me happy when people visit the mountain,” he notes.

As a hunter and outdoorswoman, I have been wearing heated socks for years. Just like my trusty heated vest, they have kept me in the field for longer, enjoying the activities I love, whether that’s tracking a whitetail or hiking with my kids. Socks are often an afterthought in the world of outdoor gear. However, they’re actually one of the most key pieces. After all, our feet play an essential role in body temperature regulation. Warm feet allow proper blood flow, moving heat to other parts of your body. When you get cold, it can make for a miserable outdoor experience—which is where heated socks come into play.

Industry observers note that while there are plenty of warm socks out there, heated socks take cozy to the next level, with rechargeable batteries powering them up. To find the warmest pairs, we tested the best heated socks for both men and women through hours of hunting, camping, and just spending time outside.

Industry observers note that these Gerbing heated socks are unlike others in that they warm up both the bottom and top of your feet via a heated microwire. My husband recently wore them on a Missouri hunt and said the only thing that kept him out there were these heated socks. With a generous battery life of up to seven hours, we never had to worry about them losing charge out in the woods and they provided more than enough warmth. Designed for comfort and performance with a moisture-wicking wool blend, these socks are ready for the elements.

According to recent reports, the sizing for these socks is unisex. We reviewed the L/XL, which fit true to size for a men’s size 10.5 wide. The heat panel runs the entire length of the bottom of the foot, providing warmth across your whole foot. If you have worn heated socks before, you know the wire can be annoying and uncomfortable. Fortunately, Gerbing used a microwire in its design for maximum comfort—no wire digging into your skin.

Recent findings suggest that these are the most expensive heated socks we reviewed; however, the quality and performance are well worth the price. Plus, the heating elements are backed by Gerbing’s lifetime warranty, so you have peace of mind.

Sources indicate that savior Heat heated socks use powerful 7.4V 2200mah rechargeable batteries to maximize warmth for hours on end. With three available heat settings, they can reach temperatures of up to 140 degrees. We like that they have a high over-the-calf design with a no-slip elastic band that keeps them securely in place. The socks are made with breathable CoolMax technology that prevents your feet from getting sweaty once they’re warm. Available in four color options, the socks come in unisex sizes to fit a range of foot shapes and sizes.

The large batteries are one of the biggest highlights of these socks. They provide a lot of power and up to seven hours of high heat on one charge. You can charge them simultaneously, and in just a few hours, they’re fully loaded and ready to go. However, they can also be a negative. Because of their size, they sometimes struggle to stay in place and can bunch up in the socks. Savior is also a good choice for the budget-conscious shopper—you can get a pair for under $80. Plus, Savior offers a 30-day money back guarantee or a free replacement should you be unhappy with your socks.

If you’re looking for the best heated socks for hunting, look no further than this pair from Snow Deer. The socks—which are available in a range of sizes and colors—come with a 7.4V battery that offers three heat settings that you can customize for as much or as little warmth as you’d like. They’re crafted from a CoolMax fabric blend that’s cozy without being stifling. Your feet will actually be able to breathe in these babies, which is important when you’re wearing your hunting boots for hours and hours.

In a recent development, the innovative heating system eliminates the feeling of wires, ensuring a seamless design and making these Snow Deer heated socks more comfortable than other options out there. They’re user-friendly, with easy temperature adjustments and charging. While they primarily heat around the toes, the socks work well in tandem with a good pair of insulated hunting boots for cold weather to help you stay outside for longer.

Recent findings suggest that actionHeat is well-known for making outstanding heated gear, and these rechargeable heated socks are no exception. They feature an ultra-fine carbon fiber heating panel that offers four levels of heat, ranging up to 140 degrees. They’re plenty warm for even the coldest of days.

The socks come with a remote control that allows you to easily adjust the heat settings while wearing them. Powered by an ActionHeat 3.74V battery along with FAR infrared heating and heat-reflective technology, they provide warmth for more than seven hours of use on a single charge. They’re made of a comfortable and stretchy cotton and spandex blend that holds up well with frequent wear. When it comes to quality, ActionHeat doesn’t skimp out.

The Ororo Mojave heated socks were designed based on valuable feedback from customers, so they have a bunch of features we appreciate. The new sock design is made with a combination of cotton, CoolMax, polyester, and spandex through a unique terry loop knitting method, which gives them a more padded and cushioned feel. Just as important, they are moisture-wicking and breathable, pulling sweat away from the skin to keep your feet dry. The breathability factor makes these socks ideal for outdoor activities like hiking or winter sports like skiing or snowshoeing.

Recent findings suggest that the heating element is located at the bottom part of the foot, providing 70 percent more coverage than Ororo’s previous model. It’s powered by 2000mAh batteries that provide up to 11 hours of use. One note: These socks are made of 60 percent cotton, so they are prone to shrinking in the wash.

According to recent reports, fieldSheer heated socks come in both men’s and women’s sizes and designs. They have a compression-like feel with ample arch support to prevent foot pain. They also sport a seamless construction, so there’s no irritation or itching. Thanks to the no-slip band, these socks never fell down while I was wearing them. In terms of comfort, I also really liked the contoured battery, which allowed the battery to fit snugly against my calf.

These Fieldsheer socks are controlled via a mobile app. There, I was able to adjust the heat setting and monitor the battery life. What’s really nice is that you can control each sock separately. Plus, you can even connect other heated gear—like heated vests or heated gloves—to the same profile. I personally really appreciated the battery life percentage monitoring capability. Even though the battery is the smallest out of all the ones we reviewed, it still lasts up to 10 hours on the lowest heat setting.

According to recent reports, with the high percentage of merino wool, these socks have a solid heat retention rating. However, they offer less coverage than others on our list—the heated area only covers from the upper part of your sole up to your toes.

According to recent reports, through years of wearing heated socks, I have narrowed down exactly what makes a quality pair. The style and comfort may fluctuate depending on the brand, but the factors below should apply to all. Of course, you’ll also want to take into consideration your own needs to make sure they’re met.

After handpicking which heated socks to include in our review process, here’s how I evaluated each pair during testing and research:.

Industry observers note that when dealing with anything that depends on battery power, the type of battery is crucial. You don’t want to invest in a pricey heated sock just for the battery to die. Rechargeable batteries are cost-effective and convenient. They are also more environmentally friendly, reducing the excess of disposable batteries in landfills.

In a recent development, however, rechargeable batteries have limited charging cycles and will require replacement. Batteries such as lithium-ion may provide more stable and reliable performance and minimize charging times.

Industry observers note that socks normally come in grouped sizing; they are “one size fits most.” Since most heated socks for men and women come up over the calf, factor your calf size into your size choice. Most of these socks are unisex, so if you have a need women’s size or a wide option, take that into consideration as you weigh your pros and cons. Always refer to the socks’ size chart to determine the best fit for your feet.

Durability is always high on my consideration list. When making a gear investment, you want something that is going to last but also that won’t break the bank. Consider the materials used. Wool, for instance, has a high heat retention rating and will last through seasons of use.

Also think about frequency of wear. What is your intended use? An avid outdoor enthusiast who aims to wear their heated socks almost daily will require a more durable option than someone who will just wear them a handful of times for weekend adventures.

Industry observers note that yes, heated socks are a great investment. I’ve worn them for years and they’re a game-changer. Of course, it also depends on your specific needs and intended use.

Sources indicate that the lifespan of your heated socks will vary depending on use and base materials. Follow the manufacturer’s instructions for washing and drying and avoid using harsh detergents to help them last longer. As for battery life, rechargeable batteries will slow down over time and start losing their charging power. Fortunately, if the sock itself is still holding up well, you can just purchase a new replacement battery to remedy that glitch.

Yes, each pair of electrical socks comes with a mesh laundry bag. Remove the batteries, cover the plug (if applicable), and clip to secure the pocket. Wash on delicate and hang to dry. That said, be sure to check the care instructions for your specific socks before washing.

Heated socks are a prime example of how advanced technology for outdoor gear has become. When choosing the best heated socks for you, weigh the performance of the batteries and the durability of the material with how comfortable the socks are. You want to get the most out of your footwear, so we recommend investing in a pair that will keep you doing the outdoor activities you love for longer, like the Gerbing Ultimate or the Snow Deer heated socks. Your feet will be happy, and so will you.

Heated Vests Are More Popular Than Ever—These Are the Best We’ve Tested

  • According to recent reports, with a heated vest, you’ll stay warm and toasty for hours longer than if you were wearing a regular vest, and you’ll get greater range of movement than a jacket.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more.

Heated vests may seem a little over-the-top, but hear us out. Unpredictable weather during the fall and early spring can make picking appropriate outdoor clothing rather challenging. It’s often too cool for summer wear, yet too warm to break out the winter jackets. Enter the vest. Not only are vests great for working outside or hunting during transition seasons, they’re also a good choice for colder temperatures—especially if you choose one that provides electric heat via a battery.

According to recent reports, with a heated vest, you’ll stay warm and toasty for hours longer than if you were wearing a regular vest, and you’ll get greater range of movement than a jacket. Stores are inundated with outerwear these days, so we did all the testing and the research for you to find the best of the best heated vests.

Sources indicate that hunters have a ton of small odds and ends, and the Ororo heated vest is a great way to organize them all. It has 14 pockets for everything from your cell phone and truck keys to extra shot shells. I love the fact that the two large front pockets utilize magnets as a closure system. This makes the vest nice and quiet for stand or blind hunting. The heating zones are be very effective at preventing heat loss, especially around the collar.

I like the fact the power button is tucked inside one of the chest pockets. It’s lighted to indicate the heating level, but it also won’t spook game since it’s tucked away out of sight. My only complaint is that Ororo doesn’t offer this vest in blaze orange. It would be great as an outer layer for safety. Plus, the vest has all the pockets to be a solid upland hunting vest. The back pocket is a little too small for larger upland birds like pheasants, but the rest of the pockets are great.

Ororo’s claim of 10 hours of battery life on low is accurate, although I expect owners will stick to medium and high. I got about 3.5 hours of runtime on high, which was slightly more than advertised. But I feel like medium is the sweet spot for the best combination of heat and runtime with this vest.

In a recent development, the Tidewe heated vest is ideal for layering because it’s thin enough to wear under a heavier jacket. This makes it easy to keep your core body temperature up during winter activities. Like the Ororo, there’s an additional zone in the collar that really helps cut down on heat loss through the neck area. The 10000 mAh battery is another plus. It allows a slightly longer runtime on the middle and high settings, which. This is an ideal vest for fishing or for watching sporting events in cold conditions.

In a recent development, one downside of the vest is that the polyester material is a bit noisy. Because of that, it might not be best for hunting unless you are planning shots at longer ranges. However, it’s hard to beat the price point of this vest. It starts at $80 and tops out at $110 depending on size. That’s a great value considering many other vests start around the $200 mark and go up from there. Tidewe—which also makes a great pair of waders—offers the vest in both black and Realtree Edge camo.

The Venture Heat ProMax is an excellent vest for men that’s both stylish and functional. During my wear test, this vest had a great fit, and kept me sufficiently warm before I ever hit the power button. Once I turned it on, the five heat zones warmed rapidly. I like the placement of all the zones. They helped to keep my core—and even my extremities—quite toasty. The vest’s simple design goes with just about all my regular fall wear and I’ve found myself reaching for it for a variety of activities.

According to recent reports, some people might not like the placement of the two battery packs on the lower back while sitting, but it was manageable for me. One minor issue I had was the power button on the lower part of the vest. Several times I bumped it without realizing it until I looked down and saw it was a different color, indicating a different setting.

Recent findings suggest that as far as battery life goes, the battery lasted for about 11 hours on the low setting. However, I feel like most people are going to utilize the high (red) setting. The runtime on high was a little over four hours, so it’s very power efficient. On the medium setting—which I found very comfortable—the battery ran for about six hours before dying.

According to recent reports, I’ve been using Gobi Heat products for a few years now and they are solid for warmth in cold weather. The Ibex heated vest is a purpose-designed work vest with five heat zones to keep your core toasty, especially when working or participating in other outdoor activities. I’ve found Gobi’s runtimes are mostly accurate, although the low settings are a bit difficult to feel if you have a ton of layers on. The battery with this vest is a little on the small side. However, it is also removable. I would pick up a spare for longer colder days.

Recent findings suggest that one of the reasons I like this vest for work is simply because it is machine-washable, so it’s going to be much easier to maintain. For anyone who spends a lot of time working construction or doing ranch work, this vest will hold up to the abuse of working day after day. I also like the power buttons on Gobi’s products. They are easy to operate while also being robust enough that you won’t turn the vest off, or change the settings if you bump it.

Arris makes an excellent heated vest that utilizes the insulating properties of fleece to trap all the warmth generated by the heat system. Fleece has some great moisture-resistant qualities that make this vest ideal for anyone planning to hunt or work in bad weather. This material is also incredibly comfortable.

This is another vest that utilizes an independent control system for the eight zones, which means you can turn the heat in for the areas you need it most. This feature alone makes this vest incredibly versatile. But it’s also thin enough to layer underneath a heavier jacket, adding to the value. The only downside we found is that the battery takes a long time to charge.

Industry observers note that the most important aspect of a heated vest is the electrical components. For the vests I tested, I charged each battery to full and then ran it until it died. I did this for multiple settings to see exactly how long they’ll keep warm in cold temperatures. I evaluated the feel of the different heat levels and how much warmth they delivered.

Additionally, I considered the following factors in picking my favorite vests.

With electric vests, the entire concept is that being keeping your core body temperature up, the rest of your body will also stay warm. It’s a simple idea, but it works provided temperatures aren’t too extreme. That’s why the heated zones of each heated vest are just about identical regardless of brand, and model. Almost every vest feature chest and back zones. Most also have heat panels in the neck area which is an area of major heat loss in most garments.

It has been revealed that used in conjunction with warm socks, a hunting jacket, or thermal underwear, a vest can be extremely effective as part of an over-all warmth system. Because vests don’t have sleeves, they do offer a greater range of movement when used alone. This makes them ideal for working or other everyday activities that require a lot of movement.

When it comes to the heating systems themselves, we highly recommend getting something with different levels of adjustment. In my experience, the lowest settings are more battery efficient, but often don’t get warm enough to feel the heat properly. Especially if you’re layered up. I usually like to use at least a 10000 mAh battery for maximum heat time while I’m working or playing outside.

The good news is that most vest batteries are interchangeable with one another. If you aren’t pleased with the stock battery’s performance, it’s usually easy to upgrade to one that gets a better runtime.

The most common construction for heated vests is a nylon outer shell that adds a certain degree of water resistance. Some people have concerns about safely wearing one of these vests in a rain. However, the voltage of these vests is far too low to be dangerous, even if the vest gets completely soaked.

It has been revealed that many heated vests feature fleece for the lining. It’s easy to maintain and absorbs odors easily. Fleece is great for working because it’s a flexible material that breathes extremely well. The downside is that it is not the most environmentally friendly.

Sources indicate that I’m also a stickler for zippers. Far too many outdoor companies have gotten cheap with these components in recent years. I personally like to look for larger zippers because they’re easier to grasp when temperatures drop. My favorites are YKK zippers because they are easy to use, and rarely get stuck on fabric or seize up.

Most vests are worn as an outer layer, but it is possible to wear clothes over thinner ones. The best option is to wear a heavier winter jacket over the vest. It depends on how many layers one wears under the vest too. Because some heated vests can get quite thick.

Sources indicate that most manufacturers advertise a maximum battery life of 12-13 hours with a power bank of this size. However, in my experience, those times usually align with a heated garment used on the low setting. Expect 6 to 8 hours with medium, and 3 to 6 hours with high for most vests. Extremely cold temperatures can negatively affect the battery life if exposed for prolonged periods.

Most people will want a heated vest to fit slightly more snugly than a normal vest. The main reason is because if the vest is loose, you might not be able to feel the heated elements. This applies for just about any heated garment. Especially when running the heat on the lowest levels. I’ve personally found that most of my heated gear needs to be run on medium at a minimum for me to feel the effects. Try to keep the layers under the vest to a minimum because that can also affect how much heat makes it to your body.

Recent findings suggest that while all the best heated vests on this list are quite capable, I liked the Venture Heat ProMax based on a combination of comfort and heating capabilities. The vest is heavy enough to work quite efficiently on its own. The stellar, battery-efficient heating system is just a bonus. In my mind, it’s the ideal fall, early winter, and spring vest for work and play.

Tech Report: Is Early-Season Skiing Worth It? Here’s the Case for Going.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s a lot to love about skiing: being outdoors, pushing yourself to improve, finding your flow, and being part of ski culture.
  • The solution is early-season skiing.
  • Plus, everything that makes skiing great still stands: you’re outside, you’re improving, you’re dipping into your flow state, and you’re more a part of ski culture than if you were to come for President’s Weekend like everyone else.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Courtesy of Vail Resorts).

There’s a lot to love about skiing: being outdoors, pushing yourself to improve, finding your flow, and being part of ski culture. But too often, the things that make skiing great get overshadowed by cost and crowds. It’s hard to find your flow when the run is crowded, and even the best ski day is hard to enjoy when lodging, lift tickets, and lunch leave you financially stretched.

The solution is early-season skiing. Few people book a ski trip in November or early December, and even local skiers tend to be unenthused. But I think they’re missing out. In fact, early season is one of my favorite times to ski. Early season turns have led to breakthroughs in my technique, and it’s one of the only times when the mountain feels small enough to meet up with friends.

Plus, everything that makes skiing great still stands: you’re outside, you’re improving, you’re dipping into your flow state, and you’re more a part of ski culture than if you were to come for President’s Weekend like everyone else.

And the things that make skiing less appealing are non-concerns.

Sources indicate that the cost of an early ski season trip can be half or even a third of what you’ll pay just a few weeks later. In Jackson Hole, for example, if you visit in early December, rather than Christmas week, you’ll pay $85 for a lift ticket instead of $340. Similarly, a room at the ultra-luxe slopeside Hotel Terra Jackson Hole increases by $600 a night based on whether you stay in early or late December. The same goes for substantial ski weeks like spring break and Presidents’ Day—and the weeks in between aren’t much cheaper.

And then there’s the fact that when you’re not skiing at the same time as everyone else, every aspect of the day (or your entire trip) becomes more enjoyable. You’ll get in more skiing thanks to shorter (or nonexistent) lift lines, and you don’t have to worry about running into someone on the way down. And when you aren’t one of 10 people waiting in line for rental gear or a table at the restaurant, you’ll get warmer, more personalized service. (Plus, in early season, everyone is fresh and excited for the season ahead, not tired and over it.).

In a recent development, when the mountain is fully open, and everyone’s ski legs are firing, the pressure to go substantial is real. It can be difficult and dangerous to try to keep up, especially if you’re latest to skiing or it’s your first (or only) ski trip of the year.

In a recent development, but in the early season, everyone is still getting their ski legs under them, and the skiing is more about fine-tuning your technique and rebuilding muscle. There’s nothing showy about it, and most people leave their egos at home.

The biggest argument against early season skiing is the lack of snow. Indeed, in the early season, the snow hasn’t had time to accumulate. Often, only the lower parts of the mountain are open, and sometimes only thanks to snowmaking. It’s not the time to do a hike-to, and you’ll rarely find any powder, so show up with your expectations (and ego) in check.

But if you’re willing to rethink what a ski day should look like, you can enjoy everything that makes skiing great while avoiding its biggest drawbacks.

Industry News: Mandatory Race Gear You’ll Actually Want to Use

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2295 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.
  • In a recent development, many ultramarathons, including Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB) require runners to carry certain gear.
  • In a recent development, mandatory trail running race equipment is a lot like American health insurance: We all hate it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

In a recent development, many ultramarathons, including Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB) require runners to carry certain gear. Cade Michael spent years as an unsponsored elite trail runner honing in his mandatory race kit with items that he both genuinely enjoys using and can be found affordably. He did this by taking advantage of sales, buying second-hand, and borrowing from friends. Here he shares his tips for building out your own race kit, including his favorite items in his pack.

In a recent development, mandatory trail running race equipment is a lot like American health insurance: We all hate it. We’re all tempted to skimp on it. And we all inevitably need it when we’re least prepared. Required gear (or most of it, anyway) doesn’t have to be a waste of money or space. After spending yeas as an unsponsored runner curating my mandatory race gear, here’s my guide to getting gear that you’ll actually want to use more than once every 365 days, including my favorite items in my pack.

Recent findings suggest that UTMB, among other races, often has extensive gear requirements and—whether you like to admit it or not—it’s usually for good reason. Weather and conditions can change rapidly in the mountains, and when you’re pushing your body to the extreme for hours (if not days) on end, as a general rule of thumb, it’s better to have it and not need it than to need it and not have it—particularly for race organizers’ liability insurance.

For example, while it may feel ridiculous for a 100K on the notoriously hot Western States 100 course in Auburn, California to make you carry a rain jacket and emergency blanket, the 2025 Canyons 100K  (on the same trails) saw snow at the start and highs around 40 degrees Fahrenheit. Packing three layers, two pairs of pants, and multiple pairs of gloves might seem like overkill for a day spent backcountry skiing in February, much less a running race in late August, but at the 2025 UTMB, ultrarunning’s most iconic race turned into a game of surviving the winter storm-like conditions.

Sources indicate that I know all too well the allure of going light. But much like Admiral Ackbar’s epiphany at the Battle of Endor, it’s (usually) a trap. At the 2026 Twisted Fork Trail Festival in Park City, Utah, weather forecasts changed drastically in the 48 hours leading into race day, projecting relentless freezing rain. I chucked on a pair of gloves and arm sleeves and figured I’d warm up plenty as the race went on. As soon as we hit the first descent I lost feeling in my hands, feet, legs, cheeks, and plenty of other places I won’t call by name. My heart rate plummeted and I struggled for the entire remainder of the day. Eventual women’s champion, Rachel Drake, on the other hand, donned a warm base layer, long tights, gloves, and vest loaded with extras. Drake is an MD/PhD, mom, and professional runner for Nike ACG. Be more like Rachel, and less like me.

But you don’t have to hate the gear you’re going to buy one way or another to participate in these events.

Quality, packable gear can not only serve to save your race should conditions take a turn through the night in the Alps, but it can also save your run or, heaven forbid, life, if you’re spending any time out on the trails. While you could probably get away with using children’s XXS sized Walmart rain pants, your niece’s tiny pinky swim goggles, and Amazon’s finest two dollar headlamp, you can also use the mandatory equipment list of your next ultra as an excuse to get quality gear that won’t sit at the bottom of your junk drawer until next summer.

Here are my tips and tricks for getting good, lasting gear that’s a little easier on your bank account than the race entry fees and international travel.

Required kit, in most cases, isn’t going to be the product you wear holes through everyday. One is built to be versatile, lightweight, and packable while the other is made for a specific purpose and durability. Some pieces of equipment, like your rain coat for UTMB, are ones you want to stand up in the most brutal of conditions. Others, like a secondary headlamp, are areas you might be able to save some weight and cash.

Lightweight, packable gear is usually updated every year just like the rest of a brand’s product line and often goes on sale during off-season months or discount days (ahem, Black Friday or REI member days). A lot of years, the only upgrade is the colorway, so just get the highlighter yellow and own it!

Better yet, buy gear second hand. Many of the products I’ll list below I grabbed from resale sites like Poshmark or Mercari for a fraction of the retail price.

It has been revealed that it may seem obvious, but always get your size. It might seem worth it to save a few grams and get a women’s XXS when you’re in the Chamonix Arc’teryx store panic-buying a rain jacket 24 hours before the gun goes off, but I promise you it’s not. Get the extra ounce and future you will be proud of the responsible decision to get something you’ll actually put on your body.

If you’re questioning whether a piece of gear will satisfy the requirements set by race organizers for your next ultra, err on the side of caution. Get the marginal gains wherever you can within reason, but I promise you trimming two centimeters off your bandaging or emergency blanket will not make Col du Grand Ferret any easier or quicker.

It has been revealed that people in your run club and or training partners have probably raced an ultra and used this stuff before. If it’s not something you will need time and time again, it’s OK to borrow it; chances are, they won’t need it in the next week or two anyway. The more you share, the more you save.

Get familiar with your equipment. Try it in training, just like you would a pair of shoes or a nutrition product. Being able to mindlessly locate and use your gear will pay dividends when you have no mindfulness left late into an ultra. Brand-spanking-latest isn’t always best.

Sources indicate that if you’re between two rain jackets, just get the one with the extra zipper. The best gear is the gear you use. Ruth Croft and Tom Evans won a historically cold and wet UTMB in 2026. When they bundled up through the night, I’m certain they were rocking the clothes they trusted to get the job done, not the ones that came in a few grams under. You’re racing an ultra marathon through the mountains, not a 5K parkrun.

Please keep reading, my opinions are important. Seriously though, whether it’s one of our gear roundups (shameless plug) or your favorite YouTuber, people put dozens of pieces through countless miles so you don’t have to. Take a few extra minutes to read a few pros and cons before you pull the trigger.

A lot of thought and stress can go into mandatory equipment, but don’t let it take away from the race experience. At my first UTMB race, UTMB Whistler in Canada, the cold-weather gear policy was implemented two days before the race due to a snowstorm. I’d just come from racing in California and Spain in September, so I didn’t have a suitcase stocked with skimpy mandatory equipment. Luckily for me, I couldn’t afford to grab a bunch of last-second gear and just used what I had with me. Retrospectively, my pack was a little heavier and bulkier than it could have been had I been properly prepared, but I didn’t think about the weight once during the race. But boy, was I glad to have warm gloves and a beanie that fit.

Here’s a list of some of my favorite mandatory equipment I’ve amassed over a couple of years of racing in Chamonix as an unsponsored athlete.

Industry observers note that this one is totally optional and, frankly, probably only applicable for a shorter ultra like MCC or OCC during UTMB week. The mini phone is a great tool to have if you’re only out for a handful of hours. So long as you ensure you get a SIM card that has roaming and data enabled for whatever country or region you will be running through, it can call, text, Whatsapp, and even Strava. UTMB requires you to have a smart phone capable of downloading and using the LiveTrail app, and this Google Play Store enabled pocket rocket is the smallest you can get while satisfying the requirements. It also takes pretty cool retro camcorder-style videos. For the longer races like CCC and UTMB, however, it’s probably your safest bet to just bring along your standard, daily driver smart phone. You have to keep your phone on at all times throughout the race, and the number of charging bricks you’d have to haul to keep this thing running through the night outsizes any weight savings it might provide.

Recent findings suggest that typically, flasks are flasks. Your running vest will usually come with a couple that fit. That being stated, I usually hate running vests. One of the primary reasons is the way traditional flasks sit in the sleeves, bouncing around and uncomfortably rubbing against my collarbone. My pro tip here is to check out flasks with smaller lids like these Hydrapak pocket flasks. Theoretically, they’re made to fit flush with your running belt, but I’ve found they are less bulky and front heavy in a running vest, too. (As long as they fit in the sleeves.).

A sure bet to be on the required kit list for almost any ultra is a waterproof rain jacket. UTMB’s specifications are rather persnickety, with required minimum waterproof rating, breathability score, sealed seams, and an integrated hood. The On Ultra Jacket lives up to demands while remaining paper thin, uber light, and incredibly packable. It can end up feeling a little too trash-baggy and unbreathable to be your workhorse running jacket, but nevertheless it’s a great piece to be able to throw in your pack anytime you head up into the unpredictable weather of the alpine.

For headlamps, I always keep a couple of options hanging around for the varying amount of daylight in different races. For OCC, for example, I opt for the Petzl E+Lite. It’s so small and light it’s an almost imperceptible item to carry and it uses nickel-sized 2432 batteries, but, as you might expect, that means it is useless for anything more than an hour or so in a pinch.

For longer races where you will inevitably be running through hours of darkness, if not the entire night, this is not somewhere to skimp on weight. A popular option in this category is the Petzl Iko Core, which features an incredible 500 lumen bulb, outstanding shine time, and a replaceable battery that sits at the back of the crown for stability. If you’re running UTMB, don’t forget to pick up the mandatory red light filter for fragile wildlife areas.

The crown jewel of mandatory equipment is the running vest. It’s what will hold all of your other mandatory equipment. It’s what will be in direct contact with your body and can make or break the convenience and comfortability of your racing experience. But, most importantly, it’s what will show up in all your post-race photos and make you look either super nerdy or really cool—by which I mean slightly less nerdy. In all seriousness, choosing your hydration vest is critical—and critically personal. Salomon and Nathan offer popular options that have dominated the category dating back to the cradle of civilization. (Hammurabi allegedly kept his chisel in an ADVskin 5L.) But the market is flooding with alternatives as the sport continues to grow, so there is no shortage of options. The most crucial things to consider are fit and layout. For my preferences, which is for my vest to feel as least like a vest as possible, the Tantrums Crest 6 and Kiprun Pro Team 5L have been excellent. The pocket layouts have tons of nooks and crannies that scratch my obnoxious need for hyperorganization better than keeping foods from touching on my Thanksgiving plate. They have minimal bounce, soft fabric across the shoulder straps, and offer a rear tunnel pocket for an extra flask. Both the Tantrums and Kiprun also come in light colors, a touch that seems a blatant choice for any piece of athletic equipment but was, until recently, a white whale on the hydration vest market.

Recent findings suggest that A good cap is indispensable and obviously extends beyond race day. It’s not that deep, just get one that feels and looks good. Ciele is a sure fire way to fit in at the coolest run club in town.

According to recent reports, waterproof pants can be a tricky one. NOAA Just Tweaked Its Winter Forecast. Here’s What’s Changed for Skiers.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (644 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Skimag

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has some encouraging news for skiers hoping for a major rebound after last winter’s dismal snow season, particularly in California and the Southwest.
  • Sources indicate that the agency’s Climate Prediction Center released its latest winter outlook on Thursday, Nov.
  • The fresh forecast tweaks a few things from its previous iterations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Courtesy of Taos Ski Valley).

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has some encouraging news for skiers hoping for a major rebound after last winter’s dismal snow season, particularly in California and the Southwest.

Sources indicate that the agency’s Climate Prediction Center released its latest winter outlook on Thursday, Nov. 19, updating its forecast for the months ahead. The biggest development? The odds of above-average precipitation have increased across California and the Desert Southwest, offering a more promising outlook for a couple of the ski regions that have struggled with snow in recent years.

The fresh forecast tweaks a few things from its previous iterations. Here’s a cheat sheet, but be sure to read on for more specifics and a regional breakdown:.

Finally, NOAA notes that the fresh precipitation forecasts are more reliable than their temperature forecasts this winter, which they attribute to the strong El Niño and an active southern storm track. In other words, there will be moisture, but there’s no guarantee it’ll come down as snow.

Here’s what the updated outlook notes:.

The latest outlook favors above-average precipitation across the southern United States, stretching from southwestern Oregon and California through the Desert Southwest and into the southern Plains and Southeast.

It has been revealed that for ski country, California and the Southwest stand out. NOAA increased the probabilities of above-average precipitation in both regions compared with its previous outlook. Southern California and southwestern Arizona now have greater than a 60 percent chance of finishing the December-through-February period wetter than average.

In a recent development, that could be welcome news for resorts in the Sierra Nevada, including Mammoth and the Lake Tahoe region, as well as Arizona Snowbowl and Newly introduced Mexico’s Taos Ski Valley and Ski Santa Fe. The forecast also offers some encouragement for southern Colorado, including Purgatory, Wolf Creek, and Telluride, although it’s far less clear for the Front Range and Northern Rockies.

It’s worth noting here that NOAA is forecasting total precipitation, not snowfall, per se. Whether that moisture falls as snow or rain will depend on temperatures, snow levels, and where individual storms track. Still, a wetter-than-average winter would be a step in the right direction.

NOAA continues to favor below-average precipitation across parts of the northern Rockies. The region also faces an increased likelihood of higher than average temperatures, a combo that’s not music to the ears of resorts in Montana, Idaho, and Wyoming. The Pacific Northwest also faces odds of warmer-than-average temperatures, particularly across Washington and Oregon.

In a recent development, elsewhere, the outlook favors wetter-than-average conditions across much of the East Coast and Southeast. However, warmer temperatures could complicate snowfall prospects, particularly at lower-elevation ski areas.

This is the latest chapter in a winter forecast that skiers have been watching closely for months. Earlier this summer, NOAA’s increasingly confident projections of a potentially historic El Niño raised hopes for a snowy rebound across parts of the West following last season’s exceptionally poor conditions.

In July, SKI spoke with meteorologists and ski-travel experts about what the developing climate pattern could mean for the upcoming season. The early consensus pointed toward the Southwest, particularly southern Colorado, Latest Mexico, Arizona, and California, as regions with favorable odds for an active storm track. Much of that remains the same.

But there were plenty of question marks, and there still are, namely what will happen in central Colorado and Utah. NOAA’s earlier outlook demonstrated average precipitation for those destinations, and the latest forecast is slightly more encouraging. We still recommend choosing higher elevation ski areas to pad your odds for snow rather than rain.

According to recent reports, NOAA’s next seasonal outlook is scheduled for December 17. Until then, skiers will have to keep watching the shorter-range forecasts and hope the promising signals translate into the kind of winter the West desperately needs.

#56297. Why Hunting Mallards in Flooded Timber is So Great

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (900 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fieldandstream ↗ Open Full Page

Why Hunting Mallards in Flooded Timber is So Great

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (900 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fieldandstream

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The best thing about timber hunting is the way ducks multiply.
  • Industry observers note that it can build until you’ve got flocks working at two or three levels, and there’s less need for calling than there is for air traffic control.
  • Two drakes peel off the bunch and backpedal into the hole.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The best thing about timber hunting is the way ducks multiply. A pair starts to circle, and that pair becomes four, then eight. Eight turn into 20. Somehow, the sight of ducks working over a timber hole draws more ducks from everywhere. It’s almost like squirrels running out onto branches to see what the others are chattering about.

Industry observers note that it can build until you’ve got flocks working at two or three levels, and there’s less need for calling than there is for air traffic control. I’ve seen that in Arkansas, but we won’t see it here—in a duck-poor state a couple hundred miles north. The two dozen mallards wheeling over our heads are as good as it’s going to get. But from where we stand, pressed tight to the trees, two dozen is more than good enough. ­Editor-​in-​chief Colin Kearns and I are doing that thing where you look down but roll your eyes up, trying to peek at ducks without flaring them, and our hearts are beating fast.

Two drakes peel off the bunch and backpedal into the hole. Travis Mueller, a Banded pro staffer, tells us not to shoot. He’s hoping the rest will follow. Kearns and I nod our heads—imperceptibly, we hope—and hold our guns ready. The rest of the ducks make one more circle, but higher and looser. Then they slide away. With the birds in the sky gone, we settle for the two in the bush. Jumping the two drakes, ­Kearns and I each shoot one. While we wish the rest had come in, the sight of these two in the trees, hanging over the decoys and lit by the morning sun, makes Kearns an instant convert to woods hunting.

Mueller, who scouts as hard as anyone, found this spot in spring by looking for beavers. Beavers plus woods equals flooded timber anywhere, and we’re standing in knee-deep water in the soft maples and willows growing between a couple of oxbow ponds. Mueller hunts here to get away from the crowds on the big water, but crowds have a habit of following successful hunters.

The first rule of timber hunting: No one talks about timber hunting. Good hunters are secretive. Mueller is a great hunter, so it’s no surprise he’s long since crossed the line from secretive to completely paranoid. We left the ramp extra early this morning to avoid detection. Even so, Mueller fretted the whole way that a couple of kids he thinks are watching him might have found his spot.

Recent findings suggest that when we got to the hole, Mueller was sure his enemies were onto him. Three hundred mallards that had been sitting here yesterday weren’t here; someone must have run them out. And the decoys were missing—no doubt, in Mueller’s mind, stolen by the competition. As Kearns and I found fallen trunks for our gear, Mueller was looking for the bag of decoys he had stashed. We could hear him sloshing and cursing in the darkness.

In traditional flooded green timber, a lack of decoys wouldn’t be a problem. Old-school hunters in Arkansas relied on calling and ripples kicked in the water to attract ducks and went without decoys. Here, though, decoys and spinners are an advantage. There are no acorns to attract ducks. Birds don’t come to flooded soft woods to eat. They want a place to hide out and loaf. The ducks we’re after are trading back and forth between a couple of refuges, or coming back to the woods after feeding in the cornfields. They need enticement. In the words of a famous timber hunter: “There are two places you can kill a duck. Where he wants to be, and where he don’t mind goin’.” This is a don’t-mind-goin’ spot, hence, the need for decoys and spinners.

When Mueller finally shines his flashlight in the right place, he finds the decoy bag. The hole is still secret. In fact, we’ll see no other hunters nor hear any shots but our own this morning. Those 300 mallards? Who knows. They were probably fresh arrivals that dropped in, then found other ducks and relocated.

With two dozen decoys in the hole and four spinners going, we’re looking good. Spinners work well in the woods, Mueller believes, because ducks lose sight of them, then see them again, as they pass over the latticework of branches. And the sun is shining. “Sun’s out, guns out” is a truism of timber hunting. Decoys show up, spinners flash, and the sun creates shadows that make it easy to hide beside a tree.

Mueller blind-calls, quacking at random intervals to whom it may concern. Often in timber hunting, you don’t see the ducks you’re calling or decoying until after they have seen you. We’re not aware of the flock until we hear the whoosh of wings overhead. When the birds drop in I miss, Kearns kills a greenhead, and Mueller shoots a bluewing drake, fully plumed, unheard of at this latitude with 10 days left in the season. It’s been a strange migration year.

We peck away at a few more, and call it a morning, being careful to pick up our hulls both because it’s what you do, and to hide any sign of our presence. For good measure, we pack the decoys out, too. A flooded hole in the woods is worth keeping secret.

#56296. Stephanie Case Just Ran 100 Miles in Antarctica. She Doesn’t Even Like the Cold.

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1536 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Trailrunnermag ↗ Open Full Page

Stephanie Case Just Ran 100 Miles in Antarctica. She Doesn’t Even Like the Cold.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1536 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 2025, a photo of Stephanie Case breastfeeding her infant daughter, Pepper, at an aid station during a 100K ultra in Northern Wales went viral, and the human rights lawyer and ultrarunner became the face of postpartum badassery.
  • Industry observers note that now, she’s officially the first woman to run 100 miles in Antarctica.
  • Recent findings suggest that “The whole idea for this race came after I had my daughter and people were asking me if I was going to start to settle down,” Case, 44, shared with Trail Runner from her home in Chamonix, France.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2025, a photo of Stephanie Case breastfeeding her infant daughter, Pepper, at an aid station during a 100K ultra in Northern Wales went viral, and the human rights lawyer and ultrarunner became the face of postpartum badassery.

Industry observers note that now, she’s officially the first woman to run 100 miles in Antarctica. Case took on the November 8 challenge in part to prove that the things she did before becoming a mom weren’t behind her. If anything, she could come back and do them even better.

Recent findings suggest that “The whole idea for this race came after I had my daughter and people were asking me if I was going to start to settle down,” Case, 44, shared with Trail Runner from her home in Chamonix, France. “They were criticizing me after I came back for my first race postpartum, telling me that I was selfish to be taking that time to train. So I wanted to go out and really prove to myself and remind myself that I could keep doing big things.”.

Actually, massive is an understatement. Of the eight runners who started the Antarctic Ice Ultra 100 miler on Union Glacier, Case was one of four finishers, and second overall. Her finishing time of 17 hours, 31 minutes and 39 seconds, a clip of 10:31 per mile, smashed the former overall course record by five hours. Only Yusheng Ni, a top ultrarunner from China with experience racing in Antarctica, ran faster in a new best-ever mark of 17:02:24.

Here’s the kicker: Case doesn’t even like running in the cold.

In a recent development, there’s cold, and then there’s Antarctica cold. The race started at 1 a.m. under a 24-hour sun, with temperatures as low as minus 35 degrees Fahrenheit—roughly 35 degrees colder than a typical kitchen freezer. And with fierce polar winds, no exposed skin is safe.

“I’m someone who doesn’t like when the house goes below room temperature. My partner and I are constantly having a fight about where we set the thermostat,” Case shared. “So this was going to be a significant challenge for me. I knew that I wasn’t going to love it. But I’m Canadian. There’s no bad weather, there’s just bad clothing, they say.”.

Finding the right gear was one of the biggest priorities in Case’s preparation. She reached out to other runners who had completed the Antarctic 100-miler in previous years to glean their insight. One offered an unexpected tip: Apply sunscreen inside of her nostrils, since the sun reflecting off the snow can burn there, too.

She also worked with The North Face, one of her sponsors, to design a custom shoe specifically for the conditions. Breathability was key: She didn’t want moisture trapped inside the shoe, and the sole needed to remain flexible in extreme temperatures. There was also the matter of laces. Frozen laces—or having to tie them with mittens on—were not an option. The solution was a BOA closure system, which let her tighten the shoes by turning a dial. The design also included an integrated, insulated but breathable gaiter and removable spikes she could screw into the soles if conditions got icy.

The setup worked better than she could have hoped. Case wore two pairs of socks—a thin liner underneath a wool pair—and didn’t change them once during the entire race.

Recent findings suggest that “I just set it and left it,” she said. “And it was one of the things I was most stressed about, because with hands, you can put on more gloves. You can have hand warmers. But toe warmers don’t work when you’re running. They can’t fit in the shoe. And I knew if my toes were cold, I was just going to be screwed. And they were toasty the whole time.”.

As for the rest of her clothing, Case had to consider another challenge: her sweat rate.

In a recent development, “I’m a heavy sweater. Even in just mild cold temperatures, I sweat a liter an hour, and in warm temperatures up to two liters,” she mentioned. “So I knew that I would be at a pretty big disadvantage, because when you sweat, your gear gets wet and then you’re screwed.”.

Industry observers note that her strategy was to dress as lightly as possible through her core while keeping her hands, feet and face warm and protected. In the coldest stretches, she wore winter tights under wind pants, along with a thin base layer, a midlayer, and a shell on top. At some points, she stripped down to a thin base layer and shell.

“As long as I kept moving, I was fine,” she mentioned. “But I wouldn’t be able to kind of stop and walk if something went wrong.”.

She never quite felt warm, and some exposed skin on her face did get frostbitten. But she managed to find moments of equilibrium.

Recent findings suggest that “I felt comfortable at times. And then other times I feel like I was just constantly on the edge,” she said. “I wasn’t freezing, but I was cold. But as long as my feet were OK and my hands were OK, then I was fine to keep moving.”.

The temperature wasn’t the only feature of Antarctica that concerned Case. She describes herself as a “mountain goat.” Living in Chamonix, she’s accustomed to steep trails and vert—not the flat, repetitive terrain of Antarctica’s 38-loop course.

Recent findings suggest that working with her coach, Meghan Roche, she shifted her training toward flatter ground and faster running. The change paid off: during her workouts, Case set personal records at several distances, from the 10K through the marathon.

“I had a love-hate relationship with it,” she noted of the training. “But the funny thing was that every time I had a training session, I was getting PRs, because I just don’t run on flat ground.”.

She also tested her gear in a cryotherapy chamber during a trip to Geneva, Switzerland, spending 20 minutes in temperatures that gradually warmed from minus 148°F to minus 22°F. The goal wasn’t so much to acclimate as to understand what the cold would feel like and test her logistics. The session made her rethink her fueling plan: Pulling off gloves, unzipping a shell, and drinking from a flask in those conditions would be too cumbersome.

Industry observers note that instead, her camera operator doubled as her crew, handing her a SIS gel and flask every loop. While most competitors visited the aid tent every lap or two, Case aimed to go ten loops—roughly a marathon—between stops. She had to cut the first stretch short when her balaclava froze into a solid block of ice, but after that she managed three 10-loop stints.

The aid station offered some reprieve, with ramen noodles, mashed potatoes, shots of maple syrup, and Rice Krispies treats, but even small tasks there got complicated. Taking her gloves off for just 30 seconds to go to the bathroom could mean waiting 20 minutes for her hands to warm up again.

Sources indicate that “There was not a single minute during this race when I kind of just relaxed and allowed myself to switch off,” she claims. “In any other 100, I can usually just kind of push past [discomfort], but there, one tiny mistake could end the race for me.”.

In a recent development, as Case recovers at home with collagen mask treatments to heal her frostbitten cheeks and nose, her next challenge is already on the calendar: becoming the first woman to complete the Montane Arctic Spine, a 500-kilometer race in February. This time, she’ll be on Nordic skis, pulling a sled and traveling solo, with checkpoints as far as 50 miles apart. She’ll need to melt her own snow, pitch her own tent, and carry out the journey without a crew.

She hopes Antarctica has prepared her for an even harder task.

“Sometimes the way to get through a really scary thing is to line up an even scarier thing afterwards,” she stated.

Beyond that, Case is developing a project called “94 Degrees,” a film that will show her running the gamut of conditions from minus 40 degrees Celsius in the Arctic to 54 degrees Celsius at Badwater in California’s Death Valley, a 94-degree Celsius spread. (She’s qualified for Badwater but still needs to apply for an invitation, so that part isn’t yet confirmed.).

It has been revealed that and in the meantime, she’ll continue her work for the U.N. while serving as the President of Free to Run, a non-profit organization that uses sport to empower women and girls in conflict-affected areas. And she’ll soak up all the cuddles she can with Pepper, now 2, while sharing stories of that one time she ran 100 miles in Antarctica. It’s a story that almost sounds like a fairy tale.

“I actually brought one of her toys, a penguin rubber ducky, with me on the trip, just as a reminder of her,” Case said. “And then this penguin came out on the course and actually ran alongside me for part of it. I’ve been showing her photos and videos … but still … it’s all kind of unbelievable.”.
